# Scampedia — full content

## Crisis: I Think I've Already Been Scammed

Source: https://scampedia.net/learn/i-think-ive-been-scammed.html
Last reviewed: 2026-08-08

## If You Sent Money — Do This First

Speed matters more here than anything else on this page. Contact whoever you sent the money through, tell them it was a scam, and ask if the payment can be stopped or reversed. Exactly who to call depends on how you paid:

- **Bank transfer or wire:** Call your bank directly, using the number on your card or bank statement — not any number the scammer gave you. Tell them it was fraud and ask if the transfer can be recalled.
- **Credit or debit card:** Call the number on the back of the card. Tell them it was fraud and ask about disputing the charge.
- **A payment app** (Zelle, Venmo, Cash App, PayPal, or similar): Contact the app's support and your bank — both. Some of these apps have fraud reporting built directly into the app itself.
- **Gift card:** Contact the company that issued the card — Amazon, Apple, Target, whichever store's name is on it — right away, and tell them the balance was part of a scam. Acting quickly sometimes lets them freeze what's left on the card.
- **A wire transfer service** like Western Union or MoneyGram: Contact them directly and ask about canceling the transfer.
- **Cryptocurrency:** Contact the exchange or wallet app you used. Crypto payments are usually very hard to reverse once sent, but it's still worth asking.

If you're not sure which of these applies, start with your bank or card company — they can often point you toward the right next call.

## If You Shared a Password, PIN, or Account Number

This is the second priority, right after the money.

Change the password on that account now, and on anything else using the same password. Turn on two-factor authentication if it isn't on already. If what you shared was a Social Security number, a bank account number, or other personal identification, that's a separate kind of exposure — a scammer can use it well after today. [IdentityTheft.gov](https://www.identitytheft.gov/), run by the FTC, walks through a personal recovery plan built around exactly what was shared.

## Report It

This matters, but it's not as time-sensitive as the two sections above — reporting can happen today or tomorrow, after the calls that actually protect your money and accounts. If you only do one of these, start with the FTC — it's the general starting point and takes a few minutes.


- **[FTC — Federal Trade Commission](https://reportfraud.ftc.gov/)** — The general starting point for reporting almost any scam — money lost, an attempt that didn't work, or anything in between.
- **[FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)](https://www.ic3.gov/)** — For scams that happened online or by email — this goes to federal law enforcement, not just a consumer database.
- **[IdentityTheft.gov (run by the FTC)](https://www.identitytheft.gov/)** — If a Social Security number, bank login, or other personal information was shared — walks through a personal recovery plan step by step.
- **[Social Security Administration Office of the Inspector General](https://oig.ssa.gov/report/)** — Specifically if the scam involved someone claiming to be from Social Security.


A local police report is also worth doing, especially if your bank or insurance later asks for one.

## This Happens to People Every Day

Scammers do this for a living. Fooling someone whose whole day involves talking to strangers, sounding official, and creating urgency isn't a sign of anything wrong with you — it's a sign the person on the other end was good at their one job. Reporting it, even if part of you would rather not talk about it, is what actually makes it harder for the same scam to work on the next person.

## Learn: Where Did This Come From?

Source: https://scampedia.net/learn/where-did-this-come-from.html
Last reviewed: 2026-08-08

## Did You Go Looking, or Did It Come to You?

This is the first question, before any other check on this site, because it costs nothing and it's almost automatic once you know to ask it.

If you searched for something and found it, or you opened an app or website you chose to open, you're in control of what you're looking at. If a text, call, email, or message arrived on its own — from a number you didn't save, an account you don't follow, a name you half-recognize — someone else decided you'd see it, at a time they picked, for a reason that's theirs, not yours. That doesn't make it fake. Plenty of real things arrive unprompted: a doctor's office confirming an appointment, a package update, a bill. But it does mean the message had a sender with an agenda, and it's worth a few seconds to notice that before doing anything it asks.

Nothing about a message's *content* tells you this — a real photo, a real name, a real logo can all arrive unprompted too. The question isn't "does this look legitimate." It's simpler and comes first: did I choose to find this, or did someone choose to send it to me.

## Who's Actually on the Other End?

The second question follows naturally from the first: if this arrived on its own, do you actually know who sent it, or do you only know who it *says* it's from?

A name in a text, a photo on a profile, a voice on a call — none of these confirm who's really there. That's not a reason to distrust every unfamiliar message. It's a reason to notice, honestly, whether you know the sender or you're taking their word for it. Those are two different situations, even when the message looks identical.

This lesson isn't where that gets resolved — [What to Do When You're Not Sure](what-to-do-when-not-sure.html) covers the actual habit for closing that gap, when it matters enough to check. What matters here is just noticing the gap exists in the first place, instead of skipping straight from "this looks like my bank" to "so this is my bank."

## This Isn't About Distrusting Everything

Most messages that arrive unprompted are exactly what they claim to be. The point of asking "where did this come from" isn't to treat every unexpected text as a threat — that would make ordinary life exhausting, and it's not what this course is asking of you.

The point is narrower: when something unprompted also asks you to do something — click, pay, share, decide quickly — that combination is worth a beat of attention that a routine appointment reminder doesn't need. Noticing where something came from is how you'll know, later in this course, which of these checks are actually worth running on it.

## Learn: Reverse Image Search

Source: https://scampedia.net/learn/reverse-image-search.html
Last reviewed: 2026-08-08

## What This Actually Tells You

A reverse image search doesn't tell you whether a photo is real or fake. What it tells you is *where else this exact photo has been* — and that's usually more useful.

If someone messages you a photo of a person claiming to be a soldier stationed overseas, a photo can't tell you by looking at it whether that's true. But a reverse image search can tell you that the same photo has been posted on a stock photography site since 2019, or that it's actually a photo of a completely different, named person's public profile. That's not a guess about pixels. That's a fact about where the image has already appeared.

This is why it's worth learning before any of the harder-to-explain AI-detection skills: it doesn't require judging anything about how the image looks. It just shows you its history.

## On Your iPhone or iPad


**Starting from a Google Images result**

1. Type what you're looking for into Google Images, the same as any search, and open the photo you want to check.
2. Press and hold your finger on the photo. A menu will pop up — tap "Search image with Google Lens."


**Starting from a photo inside a message, post, or website**

1. This works on a photo wherever you find it — a webpage, a social media post, anywhere. Open it in the Google app or Chrome. (Only have Safari? Skip to the next method below — it covers the same ground a different way.)
2. Press and hold your finger on the photo until a menu pops up.
3. Tap the search option in that menu — worded "Search inside image" in the Google app, "Search image with Google" in Chrome.
4. Scroll down to see what turns up. There's usually also a way to add a word or two if you want to narrow it down.


**Starting from a photo already saved on your phone**

1. This one works in Safari, too. Open the Google app, or open Chrome or Safari and go to google.com.
2. Tap the small camera icon inside the search box — that's Google Lens.
3. Choose the photo from your camera roll instead of taking a new one.
4. Scroll down to see what comes up.


## On a Computer


**Upload the file directly**

1. Go to google.com and click "Search by image," then "Upload a file."
2. Pick the photo from your computer and open it.


**Drag it in**

1. Find the image file wherever it's saved on your computer.
2. Drag it straight into the Google search box — no menus needed.


**Search using the photo's web address**

1. If the photo is already on a webpage, right-click it and choose "Copy image address."
2. Go to google.com, click "Search by image," and paste that address in.
3. Run the search.


**The one-click version, if you use Chrome**

1. Right-click the image directly on the page you found it on.
2. Choose "Search with Google Lens" and the results open in a panel beside the page — no need to leave it.


## What to Look For in the Results

Once you have results, you're looking for a mismatch between what you were told and what you find:

- **The photo is much older than the story.** You were told this is a photo from last week; the search shows it's been online for years.
- **The photo shows up attached to a different name.** You were told this is "Sarah from the company," but the same photo appears on a modeling site, a stock photo site, or someone else's social media under a different name entirely.
- **The photo appears on many unrelated sites.** A single, ordinary personal photo usually doesn't appear across dozens of sites. Wide reuse is a sign it was pulled from somewhere public, not taken by the person messaging you.
- **You find nothing at all.** This is genuinely ambiguous — see below.

## When It Won't Help

Reverse image search only works if the image has appeared somewhere else before, in a place a search engine has indexed. A photo that's brand new — never posted anywhere, or freshly generated by an AI tool — can come back with no matches at all. No matches doesn't mean the photo is genuine. It just means this particular check has nothing to compare against.

That's not a flaw in the tool, it's a limit worth knowing about honestly: treat "nothing found" as *inconclusive*, not as reassurance. If a photo turns up no history and something about the situation still feels off — someone you've never met asking for money, an urgent story that doesn't quite add up — the next lesson in this course, on what a message is actually asking you to do, matters more than any image check ever will.

## Learn: What Is It Actually Asking You to Do?

Source: https://scampedia.net/learn/what-is-it-asking-you-to-do.html
Last reviewed: 2026-08-09

## Four Shapes, One System

Most advice about spotting a scam focuses on the story — is the emergency real, is the photo real, is the voice real. Those questions can take a long time to answer, and sometimes can't be answered at all. There's a faster question: not "is this true," but "what is this actually asking me to do, and how is it asking me to do it."

Almost every scam request is built from the same four pieces, and they're not four separate things to individually check off — they work together, each one doing a specific job:

- **Urgency** — "before it's too late," "in the next hour," "today only." Its job is to stop you from taking the time to think or check.
- **Secrecy** — "don't tell anyone," "this needs to stay between us." Its job is to stop you from getting a second opinion from someone who'd spot it instantly.
- **Isolation** — steering you away from a specific person who'd normally help: "don't call your bank," "don't tell your husband," "your daughter can't know yet." Same job as secrecy, aimed at a specific relationship instead of everyone in general.
- **An unusual payment method** — gift cards, wire transfers, cryptocurrency, cash in the mail. Its job is to make the money impossible to get back once it's gone.

Take any one of these away and the scam usually falls apart. Take away urgency, and you have time to think. Take away secrecy or isolation, and you tell someone who says "wait, that's not how this works." Take away the unusual payment method, and even if you're fooled, the money can often be recovered. That's why real requests — from real people, real banks, real government agencies — almost never combine more than one of these at a time, and scam requests almost always combine several.

## Why a Real Photo Doesn't Change Any of This

A photo can be completely real — not AI-generated, not stolen from someone else, exactly what it claims to be — and the request attached to it can still be a scam. The photo answers a different question than the one that matters here. It might tell you the picture wasn't faked. It says nothing about whether you're being rushed, isolated, or asked to pay in a way you can't undo.

This is worth sitting with, because it cuts against the instinct this whole course exists to correct: evidence that the *content* is real doesn't tell you anything about whether the *request* is legitimate. A real photo of a real grandchild, sent by someone who has genuinely stolen their identity, attached to an urgent, secretive, wire-transfer request, is still exactly as much a scam as if the photo had been fake. Check the request, not just the evidence around it.

## Recognizing This Is the Whole Job Here

This lesson stops at recognition on purpose. Once you notice urgency, secrecy, isolation, or an unusual payment method — especially more than one at once — [What to Do When You're Not Sure](what-to-do-when-not-sure.html) covers what to actually do about it. The two matter in different ways: this is about learning to see the shape quickly, before you're already halfway into it. That one is about the one habit that gets you out.

## Learn: Content Credentials and C2PA

Source: https://scampedia.net/learn/content-credentials-and-c2pa.html
Last reviewed: 2026-08-09

## Why Absence Doesn't Mean Anything

This is the most important thing on this page, so it comes first instead of last: if you check a photo and find no Content Credentials attached, that tells you nothing. Not "probably fake." Not "worth a second look." Nothing.

There are two separate reasons for this, and either one alone would be enough. First, this is still a young standard — the camera that took most of the photos already on your phone, and the phone before that, and every photo anyone has ever sent you, never attached anything like this, because the technology didn't exist yet or the device doesn't support it. The overwhelming majority of real, ordinary, completely genuine photos in the world have never had Content Credentials and never will. Second, even a photo that started out with real credentials attached routinely loses them along the way — a screenshot captures only what's on the screen, not the original file's hidden data, so it never carries credentials at all regardless of what the original had. Saving an image from a text message, a social media post, or a messaging app frequently strips it too. The standard's own documentation acknowledges this directly: credentials "can be separated" from a file, whether by accident or on purpose.

Put those two things together and you get the honest picture: a missing credential describes almost every photo you will ever see, real or not. Treating its absence as a red flag doesn't make you safer — it makes you distrust ordinary, genuine photos for no real reason, which is exactly the trap [the lesson on visual tells](why-hands-stopped-working.html) warns about from a different angle. A check that produces false confidence in one direction is just as much a problem as one that produces false suspicion in the other.

## What It Actually Shows, When It's There

When a photo or video does carry Content Credentials, they work like a signed receipt attached to the file: what created it, what edited it, and when — checkable, not just claimed. If you open the credentials on an AI-generated image and it says so, that's a real, meaningful signal, not a guess.

The real, official tool for checking is [Content Credentials Verify](https://verify.contentauthenticity.org/), run by the Content Authenticity Initiative, the group behind the standard: upload a file or paste a link, and it shows you the credential chain if one exists. It won't tell you a photo is fake if nothing turns up — for all the reasons above, that's expected, not a red flag.

## Where This Fits With Everything Else

Content Credentials are worth checking when they're there, and worth understanding for what they can't tell you when they're not. They're not a replacement for [reverse image search](reverse-image-search.html), which works on any photo whether or not it ever had credentials attached, and they're not a substitute for [what a message is actually asking you to do](what-is-it-asking-you-to-do.html) — a photo can carry a perfectly valid credential and still be attached to a scam request that has nothing to do with whether the image itself is real.

## Learn: Why "Just Look at the Hands" Stopped Working

Source: https://scampedia.net/learn/why-hands-stopped-working.html
Last reviewed: 2026-08-08

## Why This Ever Worked

For a while, this was genuinely good advice, not a myth. Early AI image tools were bad at specific, obvious things: hands with too many fingers or fingers that bent the wrong way, text that looked like writing but wasn't actually readable, skin that came out a little too smooth or waxy. None of it was subtle. Anyone could learn to spot it in a few minutes, and for a couple of years, that was often enough to catch a fake.

## Why It Stopped

Here's the part that doesn't get said enough: those flaws were never a secret. They were the most obvious, most mocked, most talked-about problem with AI-generated images — which made them exactly the problem the companies building these tools had the strongest reason to fix first. A flaw that's famous is a flaw with a deadline.

That's roughly what happened. Hands got noticeably better. Text got better too, though it's not fully solved yet — it's just become the newest version of the same problem, and it's already improving the same way hands did. Whatever still looks slightly wrong in an image today is next on that list. It's not a permanent weakness anyone can count on staying there.

## The Real Problem With Looking for Tells at All

It's not only that the specific tells stopped working. It's that leaning on them at all teaches the wrong instinct.

If you check five fingers, count five, and treat that as your whole test, you walk away *more* confident than before you looked — confident in a photo you actually have no real reason to trust. That's worse than not checking anything. A photo you haven't checked leaves you appropriately unsure. A photo that "passed" a test that doesn't really work leaves you certain, and wrong. Wrong and certain is the dangerous combination, not wrong and unsure.

## What Actually Holds Up

None of this means there's nothing you can do about an image — it means the checks worth doing aren't about how the image looks. [Reverse image search](reverse-image-search.html) tells you where else a photo has already appeared, and that doesn't depend on whichever tool made the image ever having had a visual flaw at all. What a message is actually asking you to do, and how much urgency it's leaning on, matters more than whether a picture looks a little off.

Both of those hold up no matter which version of which tool made the image, because neither one is testing the image. They're testing everything around it — and that's something you can actually get better at with practice, in a way that staring harder at a photo never was.

## Learn: What to Do When You're Not Sure

Source: https://scampedia.net/learn/what-to-do-when-not-sure.html
Last reviewed: 2026-08-08

## The One Habit That Covers Almost Everything

You don't need to become good at spotting fakes. You need one habit: when something asks you to act immediately — send money, share a code, click a link, decide before you've had time to think — stop, and reach that person or organization again through a way you already had, not the way they just reached you.

If your grandson calls saying he's in trouble and needs money wired immediately, hang up and call him back on the number already in your phone. If a text says your bank account is locked, don't tap the link — open your banking app the way you always do, or call the number on the back of your card. If an email says you need to act on a delivery, a bill, or an account today, go to the company's website by typing it in yourself, the way you would any other day.

Almost every scam wants one thing above the money: for you to act inside the conversation it started, using only the contact information it gave you. Stepping outside that conversation is the single most useful thing you can do, and it works whether or not you can tell anything is wrong yet.

## Why This Works Even When You Can't Tell

A scammer can fake a voice, a name, a logo, an official-looking message. What they can't fake is the phone number already saved in your contacts, or the web address you type in from memory instead of clicking. The moment you leave the channel they set up and reach out on one you control, you're no longer talking to whoever wrote the message — you're talking to whoever actually answers at the real number.

This is why it matters more than being able to tell a real photo from a fake one, or a real voice from a cloned one. Those are judgment calls, made under pressure, about something designed to fool that exact judgment — and no one gets them right every time. Calling a known number isn't a guarantee either, but it replaces a judgment call with something closer to a fact: either the person you know picks up and says there's no emergency, or the actual bank says there's nothing wrong with your account.

## If You Don't Already Have a Number

Sometimes the message claims to be from an organization you don't have saved anywhere — a government agency, a delivery company, a business you've never called before. The same idea still applies: don't use any phone number, email address, or link the message gives you. Look the organization up yourself — a search you do, a bill you already have, a card in your wallet — and contact them through what you find that way.

If you can't find an independent way to reach them at all, that's information too. A real organization that needs something from you is almost always reachable through more than one route.

## Slowing Down Is Not Rude

The pressure to answer immediately is doing work for whoever sent the message, not for you. A real emergency involving someone you love will still be real in the ten minutes it takes to call them back directly. A real bill, a real account problem, a real legal notice — none of it becomes worse because you verified it first through a channel you trust. Nobody legitimate is offended by a callback.

If you take one thing from this course, take this: you don't have to get better at spotting what's fake. You just have to get in the habit of checking somewhere else before you act on it — and that habit works on everything, including the scams that haven't been invented yet.

## Scam Database: Grandparent Emergency Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/grandparent-emergency-scam.html
Category: Phone Scam
Summary: Scammers call pretending to be your grandchild in trouble — arrested, in an accident, or at the hospital — and urgently need bail money or medical fees sent via gift cards or wire transfer.
How it works: A scammer calls or texts pretending to be a grandchild in a sudden crisis — arrested, in a car accident, or hospitalized in another state or country. They beg the victim not to tell anyone else in the family "to avoid embarrassment," then hand the phone to a fake lawyer, bail bondsman, or doctor who pressures for immediate payment, almost always via gift cards, wire transfer, or a cash pickup courier — all of which are nearly impossible to trace or reverse.
Red flags: Caller insists on secrecy and tells you not to call other family members to verify. | Payment is demanded via gift cards, wire transfer, or a courier pickup — never a normal payment method. | The situation is manufactured to feel extremely urgent, leaving no time to think. | The voice sounds "a little different" but is explained away as a bad connection or a swollen jaw from the accident.
Safety tips: Never send money without calling the person directly on a number you already know. | Create a secret family code word that only your real family members would know. | Real emergencies don't require gift cards — that is always a scam. | Hang up and call your grandchild's known phone number to verify.
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Family Emergency Scams," https://consumer.ftc.gov/all-scams/family-emergency-scams

## Scam Database: AI Voice Clone Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/ai-voice-clone-scam.html
Category: AI Scam
Summary: Using just a few seconds of audio from social media, scammers clone a loved one's voice with AI and call you claiming to be in an emergency. The voice sounds completely real.
How it works: Scammers scrape a short audio clip of a target's voice from social media videos, voicemail greetings, or podcasts, then feed it into inexpensive or free AI voice-cloning software that can reproduce speech patterns after just a few seconds of source audio. Once the clone is ready, the scammer calls a family member, plays a script in the cloned voice claiming to be in a car accident, arrested, or kidnapped, and hands the call off to a fake lawyer, officer, or kidnapper who pressures for an urgent wire transfer or gift card payment before the target has time to verify what's really happening.
Red flags: The cloned voice sounds slightly flat, oddly paced, or emotionless despite the supposedly dire situation. | The call quickly hands off to a second person before the family member can be asked detailed questions. | Extreme urgency paired with instructions not to hang up or call anyone else. | Payment is requested via gift cards, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency. | The "family member" avoids or fumbles a question only the real person would know.
Safety tips: Establish a family safe word that AI cannot know — use it to verify identity. | Hang up and call back on a number stored in your own contacts. | Be suspicious of any caller who immediately asks for money. | Make your social media voice content private to limit what AI can clone.
Cited source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), 2025 Internet Crime Report, https://www.ic3.gov/AnnualReport/Reports/2025_IC3Report.pdf

## Scam Database: Fake IRS Tax Refund Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/fake-irs-tax-refund-scam.html
Category: Government Scam
Summary: Calls, texts, or emails claiming you owe back taxes and will be arrested, or that you are owed a refund that requires you to pay a processing fee first — often via gift cards.
How it works: A caller, robocall, text, or email impersonates the IRS, claiming the victim owes back taxes and will be arrested, sued, or have their wages garnished unless they pay immediately, or alternatively dangling an unexpected refund that requires paying a "processing fee" first. The message manufactures panic, directs the victim to pay via gift cards, wire transfer, or a prepaid debit card, and often spoofs caller ID to display a Washington D.C. area code or an official-looking name to appear legitimate.
Red flags: Threats of immediate arrest, deportation, or license revocation for unpaid taxes. | Demand for payment specifically via gift cards, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency. | Caller ID is spoofed to look like a government number. | Refusal to let the taxpayer ask questions or call back through an official number.
Safety tips: The IRS never calls demanding immediate payment or gift cards. | The IRS never threatens arrest over the phone. | Verify any IRS notice by calling 1-800-829-1040 directly. | The IRS contacts taxpayers by mail first, never phone or email.
Cited source: IRS.gov, "How taxpayers can protect themselves from gift card scams," https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/how-taxpayers-can-protect-themselves-from-gift-card-scams

## Scam Database: Tech Support Pop-Up Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/tech-support-pop-up-scam.html
Category: Tech Scam
Summary: A scary browser pop-up claims your computer is infected with viruses and displays a 'Microsoft' or 'Apple' phone number. Calling it connects you to scammers who request remote access to your computer.
How it works: While browsing, a victim's browser is hijacked by a malicious ad or script that displays a full-screen warning designed to look like a Windows or macOS system alert, complete with fake virus scan animations, alarming sound effects, and a phone number to call for "urgent" support. The pop-up is often built to lock or freeze the browser so it can't easily be closed, pressuring the victim to call the number, where a scammer posing as Microsoft or Apple support talks them into installing remote-access software, then charges for fake "repairs" or uses the access to steal financial information.
Red flags: A pop-up claims to be from Microsoft, Apple, or your ISP and lists a phone number to call. | The browser appears frozen or won't close normally, with a countdown timer or alarm sound. | You're asked to install remote-access software like AnyDesk or TeamViewer for a stranger. | Payment is requested via gift card, wire transfer, or a "protection plan" subscription.
Safety tips: Never call a phone number shown in a browser pop-up. | Legitimate companies like Microsoft and Apple do not make unsolicited support calls. | Close the browser tab and restart your browser to clear the pop-up. | Never allow remote access to your computer from an unsolicited caller.
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "How To Spot, Avoid, and Report Tech Support Scams," https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/how-spot-avoid-and-report-tech-support-scams

## Scam Database: Romance / Military Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/romance-military-scam.html
Category: Romance Scam
Summary: Fake online dating profiles — often claiming to be deployed military, offshore oil workers, or traveling doctors — build a relationship over weeks before creating a financial crisis requiring money.
How it works: A scammer builds a fake dating or social media profile, often using photos stolen from a real service member, doctor, or engineer, and reaches out with flattering, attentive messages that quickly escalate into a whirlwind long-distance romance. Because the persona is "deployed overseas," "on an oil rig," or "on a humanitarian mission," they always have a built-in excuse for never video calling or meeting in person, and after weeks or months of relationship-building they introduce a sudden financial emergency and ask the victim to wire money or buy gift cards.
Red flags: The relationship moves to declarations of love very quickly despite never meeting in person. | Consistent excuses to avoid video calls or in-person meetings. | A sudden financial emergency requiring money to be wired or sent via gift cards. | Profile photos are professionally lit, model-like, or reused across other profiles.
Safety tips: Never send money to someone you have not met in person. | Do a reverse image search on their profile photos — they are often stolen. | Be suspicious of anyone who refuses to video chat or always cancels. | Deployed US military personnel have access to military banking and don't need money wired.
Cited source: Military Consumer (FTC-affiliated), "Military Consumers and Romance Scams," https://www.militaryconsumer.gov/blog/military-consumers-romance-scams

## Scam Database: Crypto Investment Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/crypto-investment-scam.html
Category: Investment Scam
Summary: Promises of guaranteed high returns on cryptocurrency or forex investments, often introduced through social media, fake apps, or romance relationships. Victims lose everything when they try to withdraw.
How it works: Victims are approached through social media ads, unsolicited messages, or an online relationship by someone who presents themselves as a savvy crypto trader with a "proven" strategy or exclusive platform. The scammer directs the victim to a slick-looking trading app or website that shows a small initial investment growing rapidly, encouraging larger deposits. When the victim eventually tries to withdraw, the platform demands additional "taxes," "fees," or "verification deposits," and once those are paid it either disappears or keeps stalling indefinitely.
Red flags: Guaranteed or unusually high, consistent returns with little to no risk. | Pressure to invest more money right as you try to withdraw. | Unexpected fees or taxes required before a withdrawal can be processed. | The platform or advisor was found through an unsolicited message or online romantic contact.
Safety tips: No legitimate investment guarantees returns — that claim is always a lie. | Verify any investment firm with the SEC at investor.gov or FINRA at BrokerCheck. | Never invest money you cannot afford to lose completely. | If someone you met online is suggesting investments, that is a major red flag.
Cited source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), "The FBI Warns of a Spike in Cryptocurrency Investment Schemes," https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2023/psa230314

## Scam Database: Medicare / Health Insurance Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/medicare-health-insurance-scam.html
Category: Government Scam
Summary: Callers pretend to be from Medicare or a health insurance company offering free equipment or coverage updates, then steal your Medicare number to commit fraud and bill for services you never received.
How it works: A caller claims to represent Medicare or a health insurance company and offers something enticing — free genetic testing, a back or knee brace, or an updated Medicare card — but needs to "verify" the victim's Medicare number and other personal details first. The stolen Medicare number is then used to submit fraudulent claims for equipment or services the victim never received, which can max out benefits and complicate coverage for legitimate future care.
Red flags: An unsolicited call or text offering free medical equipment or a "new" Medicare card. | A request to confirm your Medicare number over the phone. | Pressure to accept a product or service you didn't ask for. | Claims to be a Medicare representative but calls from an unfamiliar or spoofed number.
Safety tips: Medicare will never call you asking for your Medicare number. | Guard your Medicare number like a credit card number. | Review your Medicare Summary Notice for charges you don't recognize. | Report suspected fraud to 1-800-MEDICARE.
Cited source: HHS Office of Inspector General, "Fraud Alert: Genetic Testing Scam," https://oig.hhs.gov/fraud/consumer-alerts/fraud-alert-genetic-testing-scam

## Scam Database: Lottery / Prize Notification Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/lottery-prize-notification-scam.html
Category: Phone Scam
Summary: You receive a letter, call, or email claiming you've won a lottery or sweepstakes you never entered. To claim the prize you must first pay taxes, fees, or customs charges upfront.
How it works: The victim receives a letter, phone call, or email announcing they've won a large cash prize, foreign lottery, or sweepstakes, often referencing a contest they don't remember entering. To "release" the winnings, they're told to first pay taxes, customs duties, insurance, or a processing fee, usually via wire transfer or gift card, and once that payment is sent the scammer either disappears or invents another fee, repeating the cycle for as long as the victim keeps paying.
Red flags: Notification of winning a contest or lottery you never entered. | A requirement to pay fees or taxes before receiving the prize. | Payment requested via gift card, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency. | Urgency to claim the prize within a short deadline.
Safety tips: You cannot win a contest you never entered. | Legitimate prizes never require upfront fees or taxes to claim. | Winning notifications are never sent by email, phone, or letter. | The only real lottery is one you purchased a ticket for yourself.
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Don't pay for a prize (scam)," https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2025/06/dont-pay-prize-scam

## Scam Database: Wangiri / One-Ring Callback Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/wangiri-one-ring-callback-scam.html
Category: Phone Scam
Summary: A call rings once from an unfamiliar international number and hangs up before you can answer, banking on curiosity making you call back. The returned call connects to a premium-rate line that racks up enormous per-minute charges, a cut of which goes to the scammer.
How it works: An automated system dials thousands of numbers and lets each ring exactly once before hanging up, leaving a missed call from an unfamiliar international number. Curious or concerned victims call back, unknowingly connecting to a premium-rate number set up by the scammer, and the call is deliberately kept going with hold music, fake menus, or a "please stay on the line" recording so it racks up per-minute international charges, a portion of which is paid out to whoever set up the number.
Red flags: A missed call from an unfamiliar international number that only rang once. | An unrecognized country code, especially ones associated with premium-rate scams. | The callback connects to hold music, silence, or a confusing automated menu that stalls. | An unusually large charge for a single international call appears on your phone bill.
Safety tips: Don't call back unfamiliar international numbers, especially after just one ring. | Check the country code before dialing back — unrecognized codes are a red flag. | Block and report the number instead of returning the call. | Contact your carrier if you're billed for a call you never intentionally placed.
Cited source: Montgomery County (MD) Police Department, "One Ring Scam," https://www.montgomerycountymd.gov/montgomery-county-police-department/how-do-i/frauds-scams/one-ring-scam

## Scam Database: "Can You Hear Me?" Robocall Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/can-you-hear-me-robocall-scam.html
Category: Phone Scam
Summary: A robocall or live scammer opens with a simple yes-or-no question like "can you hear me?" hoping to record you saying "yes," which they claim can later be used to authorize charges you never agreed to.
How it works: A robocall or live scammer opens with an innocuous-sounding question such as "Can you hear me?" hoping the victim instinctively answers "yes." Scammers have claimed a recorded "yes" can be spliced together with an unrelated recorded question to fake consent for a purchase or service the victim never agreed to. Whether the direct fraud through this exact recording is common has been debated by researchers, but the tactic remains widely used as an opener to keep victims engaged for further social engineering.
Red flags: The call opens with a simple yes/no question from an unfamiliar or robotic-sounding caller. | The caller pushes to keep you talking and answering questions after the opener. | The number calling appears local but doesn't match anyone you know (neighbor spoofing). | You're later asked to confirm personal or account information on the same or a follow-up call.
Safety tips: Simply hang up on robocalls instead of engaging, even to say "no." | Answer with a neutral greeting rather than "yes" or "no" if you must respond. | Never confirm personal details to an unsolicited caller, recorded or not. | Register your number on the National Do Not Call Registry to cut down on robocalls.
Cited source: Minnesota Attorney General's Office, "'Can You Hear Me?' Scam Calls," https://www.ag.state.mn.us/consumer/Publications/CanYouHearMe.asp

## Scam Database: Fake Bank Fraud Alert Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/fake-bank-fraud-alert-scam.html
Category: Phone Scam
Summary: A text or call appears to come from your bank warning of suspicious activity and asks you to "verify" your account by providing your card number, PIN, or a one-time passcode — information a real bank never requests this way.
How it works: A text or spoofed phone call appears to come from the victim's real bank, warning of a suspicious charge or login attempt and asking them to "verify" their identity. The victim is directed to reply to the text, click a link to a fake bank login page, or stay on the phone with a fake "fraud department" representative, who then asks for the debit card number, PIN, or a one-time passcode the bank just sent by text — a code that, once handed over, lets the scammer complete a real transaction or password reset on the victim's actual account.
Red flags: An unsolicited text or call about a "fraud alert" asking you to confirm account details. | A request for a one-time passcode you just received by text. | Caller ID spoofed to display your real bank's name or number. | Urgency to act immediately to "stop" a charge that supposedly is in progress.
Safety tips: Hang up and call the number on the back of your card, never a number from the text or call itself. | Never share a one-time passcode with anyone, even someone claiming to be your bank. | Banks never ask for your full PIN or password over phone or text. | Log in directly through your bank's official app or website to check for real alerts.
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Got a call about fraud activity on your bank account? It could be a scammer," https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2024/06/got-call-about-fraud-activity-your-bank-account-it-could-be-scammer

## Scam Database: Jury Duty Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/jury-duty-scam.html
Category: Government Scam
Summary: A caller claims to be a sheriff or court officer saying you missed jury duty and now face arrest unless you immediately pay a fine — usually via gift cards or a prepaid card — to avoid being taken into custody.
How it works: A caller impersonating a sheriff's deputy or court officer tells the victim they missed a jury duty summons and now have an active warrant for their arrest, which can only be resolved by immediately paying a fine. The caller uses official-sounding titles, badge numbers, and case numbers to sound credible, insists the payment must be made right away via gift cards or a prepaid debit card to avoid being taken into custody, and often warns the victim not to hang up or contact the courthouse directly while the "payment" is processed.
Red flags: A claim that you'll be arrested imminently unless you pay a fine right now. | Payment demanded through gift cards or a prepaid card. | Instructions not to hang up or verify the claim by calling the courthouse yourself. | Use of official-sounding badge or case numbers to sound legitimate.
Safety tips: Courts never demand payment over the phone to avoid arrest. | Gift cards are never a legitimate form of payment for any government fee or fine. | Hang up and call your local courthouse directly using a number you look up yourself. | Law enforcement does not call ahead to warn of an imminent arrest.
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Did you get a call or email saying you missed jury duty and need to pay? It's a scam," https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2024/09/did-you-get-call-or-email-saying-you-missed-jury-duty-and-need-pay-its-scam

## Scam Database: Social Security Number Suspended Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/social-security-number-suspended-scam.html
Category: Government Scam
Summary: An automated call or voicemail claims your Social Security number has been "suspended" due to suspicious activity and instructs you to press a number or call back, aiming to extract your SSN and other personal details.
How it works: An automated call or voicemail claims the victim's Social Security number has been linked to criminal activity and "suspended," instructing them to press a number to speak with an "agent." The agent claims the only way to protect their remaining benefits or avoid arrest is to verify their SSN, date of birth, and bank information, or to move their money to a "safe" government-controlled account — which is really an account the scammer controls, or simply a pretext to collect enough personal data to commit identity theft.
Red flags: A claim that your Social Security number has been "suspended" — this isn't something SSA does. | Pressure to confirm your SSN or bank details over an unsolicited call. | Instructions to move money into a new or "safe" account. | Threats of arrest or loss of benefits for not complying immediately.
Safety tips: The Social Security Administration cannot suspend your number and will never call to tell you so. | Never give your Social Security number to an unsolicited caller. | Hang up and call the SSA directly using their official number to check your account status. | Report suspicious calls to the SSA Office of the Inspector General.
Cited source: Social Security Administration, "Protect Yourself from Social Security Scams," https://www.ssa.gov/scam/

## Scam Database: Unemployment Benefits Identity Theft Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/unemployment-benefits-identity-theft-scam.html
Category: Government Scam
Summary: Criminals use stolen personal information to file fraudulent unemployment claims in a victim's name, often surfacing only when the real person receives a tax form for benefits they never applied for or received.
How it works: Using personal information stolen in prior data breaches or phishing scams, criminals file a fraudulent unemployment claim in the victim's name with a state labor agency, directing payments to a bank account or prepaid card they control. Because the application is filed remotely and states have often been overwhelmed with claim volume, the fraud usually isn't caught until the real person receives a 1099-G tax form reporting benefits income they never applied for or received, or their actual employer gets a notice about a claim filed while they were still working.
Red flags: Receiving a 1099-G tax form for unemployment benefits you never claimed. | A notice from your state unemployment office about a claim you didn't file. | Your employer receives a claim notice while you're still actively employed. | Unexplained mail from unfamiliar state unemployment agencies.
Safety tips: Check your credit report regularly for unfamiliar accounts or inquiries. | If you receive an unexpected tax form for benefits you never claimed, report it to your state unemployment office immediately. | Freeze your credit with the three major bureaus if you suspect identity theft. | File a report with the FTC at IdentityTheft.gov if you're a victim.
Cited source: U.S. Department of Labor, "Report Unemployment Identity Fraud," https://www.dol.gov/agencies/eta/UIIDtheft

## Scam Database: Student Loan Forgiveness Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/student-loan-forgiveness-scam.html
Category: Government Scam
Summary: Companies advertise guaranteed student loan forgiveness or dramatically reduced payments for an upfront fee, then either do nothing, enroll borrowers in a plan they could have gotten for free, or steal the login credentials used to "help."
How it works: A company advertises through social media, robocalls, or email claiming to offer guaranteed loan forgiveness, dramatically reduced payments, or enrollment in a "limited-time" federal program, and asks for an upfront enrollment fee or monthly payment routed through them instead of the real loan servicer. In many cases the company simply enrolls the borrower in an income-driven repayment plan they could have signed up for free directly with their servicer, or it collects the victim's FSA ID and login credentials and uses them to redirect the loan account or apply for aid fraudulently.
Red flags: A request for an upfront fee to apply for loan forgiveness or consolidation. | Claims of a "limited-time" or "special" government program you must act on immediately. | A request for your Federal Student Aid (FSA) ID or password. | Contact came from an unsolicited call, text, or social media ad rather than your actual loan servicer.
Safety tips: Legitimate loan forgiveness and repayment programs are always free to apply for directly through your loan servicer. | Never pay an upfront fee for loan forgiveness or consolidation help. | Never share your Federal Student Aid (FSA) ID with a third party. | Verify any offer directly at StudentAid.gov.
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Scammers follow the news about student loan forgiveness," https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2024/04/scammers-follow-news-about-student-loan-forgiveness

## Scam Database: USCIS / Immigration Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/uscis-immigration-scam.html
Category: Government Scam
Summary: Scammers posing as immigration officials contact applicants claiming a fee must be paid immediately by phone to avoid deportation or a denied application, exploiting fear around immigration status.
How it works: A scammer posing as a USCIS official, immigration attorney, or ICE agent contacts an applicant or their family, claiming there's a problem with their immigration case — a missing fee, an error in paperwork, or an impending deportation — that can only be resolved by paying immediately over the phone. The caller exploits fear around immigration status to pressure quick, untraceable payment via gift cards or wire transfer, sometimes spoofing caller ID to show a Washington D.C. number or referencing real USCIS form numbers to sound credible.
Red flags: A demand for payment over the phone to resolve an immigration case. | Threats of immediate deportation or denial unless you pay right away. | Payment requested via gift cards or wire transfer. | Caller ID spoofed to appear as a government agency.
Safety tips: USCIS does not accept payment over the phone or via gift cards. | Government agencies communicate official actions by mail, not urgent phone calls. | Verify your case status directly on the official USCIS website. | Consult a licensed immigration attorney if you're unsure about a communication.
Cited source: USCIS, "Common Scams," https://www.uscis.gov/scams-fraud-and-misconduct/avoid-scams/common-scams

## Scam Database: Phishing Email Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/phishing-email-scam.html
Category: Tech Scam
Summary: A fraudulent email impersonates a trusted company or contact, urging the recipient to click a link and log in on a fake page that steals their username and password, or to open an attachment that installs malware.
How it works: An email is crafted to look like it comes from a trusted company, coworker, or service — spoofing the sender name and copying real logos and formatting — and creates a reason to click a link, such as a "suspicious login," an invoice, or an account suspension warning. The link leads to a convincing fake login page that captures whatever username and password the victim enters, or the email carries an attachment that installs malware when opened, giving the attacker access to accounts, files, or the ability to launch further attacks from the victim's own contacts.
Red flags: The sender's actual email address doesn't match the company it claims to be from. | A generic greeting like "Dear Customer" instead of your actual name. | Urgent language about account suspension, security alerts, or unpaid invoices. | A link that, when hovered over, points to an unfamiliar or misspelled domain.
Safety tips: Hover over links to check the real destination before clicking. | Look closely at the sender's actual email address, not just the display name. | Never enter your password after clicking a link in an unsolicited email. | Enable two-factor authentication so a stolen password alone isn't enough to break in.
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "How To Recognize and Avoid Phishing Scams," https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/how-recognize-avoid-phishing-scams

## Scam Database: Smishing Text Message Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/smishing-text-message-scam.html
Category: Tech Scam
Summary: Phishing conducted over SMS text message, often impersonating a delivery service, bank, or government agency with a link to a fake site designed to steal login credentials or payment information.
How it works: A text message impersonates a delivery company, bank, or government agency and includes a link claiming there's a problem to resolve — an undeliverable package, a locked account, or an unexpected charge. Tapping the link leads to a fake website designed to look like the real company's site, where the victim is prompted to "log in" or enter payment details, handing their credentials or card number directly to the scammer.
Red flags: An unexpected text about a delivery, bank issue, or bill with a link to click. | The link uses a shortened or unfamiliar URL rather than the company's real domain. | Poor grammar, odd spacing, or a sense of urgency in the message. | A request to enter a password or one-time code on the linked page.
Safety tips: Don't tap links in unexpected text messages, even if they look official. | Go directly to the official app or website instead of using a link from a text. | Forward suspicious texts to 7726 (SPAM) to report them, then delete. | Never enter a one-time passcode on a page you reached through a text link.
Cited source: Federal Communications Commission, "How to Identify and Avoid Package Delivery Scams," https://www.fcc.gov/how-identify-and-avoid-package-delivery-scams

## Scam Database: QR Code Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/qr-code-scam.html
Category: Tech Scam
Summary: A malicious QR code — placed over a legitimate one on a parking meter, menu, or poster, or sent digitally — redirects victims to a fake payment or login page designed to steal money or credentials.
How it works: A scammer prints a fraudulent QR code sticker and places it over a legitimate one on a parking meter, restaurant menu, or event poster, or sends one directly in an email or flyer. Scanning it redirects the victim to a fake payment or login page that looks like the real service, where they're prompted to enter card details or account credentials that go straight to the scammer instead of the intended business.
Red flags: A QR code sticker looks slightly crooked or pasted over another one. | The scanned link leads to a generic-looking or misspelled payment page. | The QR code was in an unsolicited email, text, or unattended public flyer. | You're asked for card details on a page that doesn't match the business's usual branding.
Safety tips: Check for a sticker placed over another QR code before scanning in public. | Preview the destination URL before opening it, if your camera app supports it. | Avoid entering payment or login details on a page reached by scanning an untrusted QR code. | Use the official app or website directly instead of scanning when possible.
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "See a QR code parked somewhere? Don't scan it...yet!" September 2026, https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/09/see-qr-code-parked-somewhere-dont-scan-ityet

## Scam Database: Fake Antivirus / Scareware Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/fake-antivirus-scareware-scam.html
Category: Tech Scam
Summary: A pop-up or fake scan result falsely claims your device is riddled with viruses and pressures you to buy bogus security software or call a "support" number, which leads straight into a tech support scam.
How it works: A pop-up ad or malicious website displays a fake "scan" that rapidly fills the screen with alarming red warnings claiming dozens of viruses were found. It urges the victim to immediately purchase a specific antivirus program to "clean" the device, and paying often either does nothing, installs real malware disguised as security software, or funnels the victim into calling a number that leads directly into a tech support scam where a scammer requests remote access.
Red flags: A pop-up claims to have already scanned your device and found viruses. | Flashing warnings, sirens, or a countdown pressuring immediate purchase. | A prompt to buy security software directly from the pop-up itself. | A phone number displayed to call for "immediate removal."
Safety tips: Real antivirus software doesn't sell itself through browser pop-ups. | Close the browser tab or restart your device rather than clicking anything in the pop-up. | Only install security software directly from a vendor's official website. | Run a scan with security software you installed yourself if you're worried about infection.
Cited source: Federal Trade Commission, "Operator of Deceptive 'Scareware' Scheme Will Pay More than $8 Million to Settle FTC Charges," https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2011/01/operator-deceptive-scareware-scheme-will-pay-more-8-million-settle-ftc-charges

## Scam Database: Social Media Account Takeover Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/social-media-account-takeover-scam.html
Category: Tech Scam
Summary: A hacked or cloned social media account messages the victim's friends and family asking for money, gift cards, or a "favor" verification code, exploiting the trust of an existing relationship.
How it works: A scammer gains access to a real person's social media account, usually through a prior phishing link or a reused, breached password, then messages the account's friends and family from inside the trusted account. Posing as the real owner, they claim to be in a bind and ask for a quick loan, gift cards, or help receiving a "verification code" that's actually the code needed to take over the recipient's own account next, spreading the takeover through the victim's social circle.
Red flags: A friend suddenly asks for money or gift cards through a direct message. | A request to share a verification code you just received by text. | The message doesn't sound like how your friend normally writes. | The friend is unreachable by phone or other means to confirm the request.
Safety tips: Call or video chat to confirm identity before sending money to anyone contacting you on social media, even a close friend. | Never share a login verification code you receive by text, even if a friend asks for it. | Enable two-factor authentication on all of your social accounts. | Report and alert your contacts immediately if your account is compromised.
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "That friend request could be from a scammer," https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2023/10/friend-request-could-be-scammer

## Scam Database: SIM Swap Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/sim-swap-scam.html
Category: Tech Scam
Summary: A scammer convinces your mobile carrier to transfer your phone number to a SIM card they control, letting them intercept the text-message codes used to reset passwords and drain bank or crypto accounts.
How it works: A scammer gathers enough personal information about a target — often through phishing or data broker sites — to impersonate them to their mobile carrier, either by calling customer support or tricking an employee, and requests that the victim's phone number be transferred to a new SIM card the scammer controls. Once the swap goes through, the victim's phone loses service entirely while the scammer starts receiving all their calls and texts, including the one-time passcodes needed to reset passwords on email, banking, and cryptocurrency accounts.
Red flags: Your phone suddenly loses all signal or shows "No Service" with no explanation. | You stop receiving calls or texts you were expecting. | You get a notification that your SIM or phone number was changed without your action. | You're locked out of accounts that use text messages for two-factor authentication.
Safety tips: Add a PIN or passcode to your mobile account that's required for any SIM changes. | Use an authenticator app instead of SMS for two-factor authentication where possible. | Watch for an unexpected loss of cell signal, which can indicate your number was just transferred. | Contact your carrier immediately if your phone suddenly loses service without explanation.
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "SIM Swap Scams: How to Protect Yourself," https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2019/10/sim-swap-scams-how-protect-yourself

## Scam Database: Virtual Kidnapping Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/virtual-kidnapping-scam.html
Category: AI Scam
Summary: A caller claims to be holding a family member hostage and demands an immediate ransom payment, sometimes using an AI-cloned voice of the "victim" crying for help, even though the person is actually safe.
How it works: A scammer calls claiming to be holding a family member hostage, often having researched the victim's family and travel plans online to sound convincing, and sometimes plays a recording or AI-cloned voice of a person crying or screaming for help in the background. The caller demands an immediate wire transfer or gift card payment to secure release and insists the victim stay on the phone continuously and not contact police or try to reach the "kidnapped" person, all while that person is actually safe and completely unaware a call is taking place.
Red flags: A caller demands you stay on the line continuously and not hang up to check on anyone. | Instructions not to contact police under threat of harm to the "hostage." | Immediate demand for ransom via wire transfer or gift cards. | The "kidnapped" person's voice sounds distorted, distant, or slightly off.
Safety tips: Try to contact the supposedly kidnapped person directly on their own phone before doing anything else. | Stay calm and ask questions only the real person would know the answer to. | Never wire money or buy gift cards based on a phone threat alone. | Contact local police immediately — they have protocols for these calls.
Cited source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), "Criminals Using Altered Proof-of-Life Media to Extort Victims in Virtual Kidnapping for Ransom Scams," https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA251205

## Scam Database: Deepfake Celebrity Endorsement Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/deepfake-celebrity-endorsement-scam.html
Category: AI Scam
Summary: AI-generated video or audio shows a celebrity or public figure appearing to endorse an investment platform, giveaway, or product they have never actually endorsed, used to lend false credibility to a scam.
How it works: Scammers use AI video and voice generation tools to create a fake but convincing clip of a well-known celebrity, news anchor, or business figure appearing to endorse a cryptocurrency platform, investment opportunity, or giveaway. The video is spread through social media ads or fake news articles, lending false credibility that pressures viewers to sign up and deposit money on a platform that has nothing to do with the celebrity and is really just designed to collect and keep victim deposits.
Red flags: A celebrity appears to endorse an investment or giveaway only in an ad or shared video. | The celebrity's own official channels make no mention of the endorsement. | Slight glitches in lip-sync, unnatural blinking, or robotic-sounding audio. | The ad links to an unfamiliar trading platform or "double your money" giveaway.
Safety tips: Be skeptical of any celebrity "endorsement" for a financial product seen only in an ad or video. | Check the celebrity's own verified social accounts or official site for confirmation. | Look for subtle glitches in lip-sync, lighting, or audio that can reveal an AI fake. | Remember that real investment opportunities are never promoted through unsolicited video ads.
Cited source: Federal Trade Commission, "FTC Proposes New Protections to Combat AI Impersonation of Individuals," February 2024, https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/02/ftc-proposes-new-protections-combat-ai-impersonation-individuals

## Scam Database: AI Chatbot Romance Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/ai-chatbot-romance-scam.html
Category: AI Scam
Summary: An AI-powered chatbot, sometimes on a dating app, carries on a convincingly personal conversation for weeks or months before steering the victim toward sending money, gifts, or investing in a fraudulent scheme.
How it works: A scammer deploys an AI chatbot on a dating app or messaging platform, sometimes paired with an appealing stolen profile photo, to carry on an engaging and emotionally responsive conversation around the clock. Because the bot can chat instantly at any hour and adapt its tone to keep the victim interested, it builds a sense of closeness over weeks before steering the conversation toward a financial ask — a crypto "investment opportunity," travel money, or gifts — sometimes with a human operator taking over once the victim is emotionally invested enough to pay.
Red flags: Replies come instantly at all hours, even very late at night. | Conversation feels emotionally intense very quickly but avoids specific, personal follow-ups. | The match consistently avoids or postpones video calls. | The relationship eventually pivots toward an investment tip or financial request.
Safety tips: Be cautious of a match who is available to chat constantly at all hours but avoids calls or video. | Watch for oddly generic or repetitive phrasing that can indicate an automated response. | Never send money or financial details to someone you've only spoken to online. | Ask specific, personal follow-up questions that a scripted bot is likely to answer inconsistently.
Cited source: Federal Trade Commission, "FTC Launches Inquiry into AI Chatbots Acting as Companions," September 2025, https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/09/ftc-launches-inquiry-ai-chatbots-acting-companions

## Scam Database: Catfishing Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/catfishing-scam.html
Category: Romance Scam
Summary: Someone creates a fake online identity, often using stolen photos of an attractive stranger, to build a relationship for emotional manipulation, financial gain, or simply to deceive without necessarily asking for money.
How it works: Someone builds a fake online persona using photos and details stolen from a real person's social media, then reaches out to targets on dating apps, social media, or messaging platforms to build a relationship under the false identity. The motive varies — some catfish for financial gain, some for emotional validation or control, and some simply to deceive without ever asking for money — but the relationship is built entirely on a fabricated identity that unravels under any real scrutiny, like a video call or an in-person meeting.
Red flags: Profile photos look professionally shot or model-quality for an average dating profile. | Inconsistent details about their job, hometown, or daily life across conversations. | Constant excuses to avoid meeting in person or video chatting. | A reverse image search shows the photos belong to someone else entirely.
Safety tips: Reverse image search profile photos to check if they've been stolen from someone else. | Insist on a live video call early in any online relationship. | Be wary of inconsistent details about their job, location, or life story. | Trust your instincts if something about their story doesn't add up.
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "What To Know About Romance Scams," https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/what-know-about-romance-scams

## Scam Database: Sextortion Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/sextortion-scam.html
Category: Romance Scam
Summary: A scammer coerces or tricks a victim into sharing intimate photos or video, then threatens to release them to friends, family, or publicly unless paid, often escalating demands after the first payment.
How it works: A scammer, often posing as an attractive stranger, quickly builds rapport online and convinces the victim to share intimate photos or video, or in some cases records a video call without the victim's knowledge or uses a fabricated image. Once they have the material, the scammer reveals their real intent, threatening to send the images to the victim's friends, family, or employer unless a payment is made, and frequently continues demanding more money even after the first payment is sent.
Red flags: A new online contact pushes quickly toward exchanging intimate photos or video. | A sudden shift from friendly conversation to threats and demands for payment. | Screenshots or a list of your social media contacts are shown as proof they can reach them. | Demands continue or increase even after a payment is made.
Safety tips: Stop all contact and payment — paying rarely stops the threats and often increases them. | Report the account to the platform and preserve evidence with screenshots. | Contact the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children or local law enforcement, especially if a minor is involved. | Remember you are the victim of a crime, not someone at fault for being deceived.
Cited source: FBI, "Sextortion," https://www.fbi.gov/how-we-can-help-you/scams-and-safety/common-frauds-and-scams/sextortion

## Scam Database: Ponzi Scheme

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/ponzi-scheme.html
Category: Investment Scam
Summary: An investment scheme pays early investors with money from new investors rather than actual profit, creating the illusion of a successful business until new money stops flowing in and the scheme collapses.
How it works: An operator collects money from investors while promising steady, above-market returns, but instead of investing the funds in any real business, they simply pay "returns" to earlier investors using money deposited by newer ones. The scheme can appear legitimate for months or years as long as enough new money keeps coming in to cover withdrawals, but it inevitably collapses once new investment slows or a large number of investors try to cash out at once, leaving most participants with total losses.
Red flags: Consistently high returns that don't fluctuate with overall market conditions. | Vague or overly complex explanations of how the investment actually makes money. | Pressure to recruit other investors as part of the opportunity. | Difficulty or delays when trying to withdraw funds.
Safety tips: Be suspicious of consistently high returns regardless of market conditions. | Verify any investment manager is registered with the SEC or your state securities regulator. | Ask how the underlying business actually generates the returns being promised. | Be cautious of pressure to recruit new investors as part of the "opportunity."
Cited source: Investor.gov (U.S. SEC), "Ponzi Schemes," https://www.investor.gov/additional-resources/general-resources/glossary/ponzi-schemes

## Scam Database: Pump and Dump Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/pump-and-dump-scam.html
Category: Investment Scam
Summary: Promoters hype a low-value stock or cryptocurrency through social media and unsolicited messages to inflate its price, then sell their own holdings at the peak, leaving new buyers with a worthless investment.
How it works: A group of promoters accumulates shares of a low-value, thinly traded stock or a new cryptocurrency token, then floods social media, messaging groups, and unsolicited emails with hype claiming the price is about to explode. As unsuspecting buyers rush in and drive the price up, the promoters quietly sell their own holdings at the inflated price, and once they've cashed out the promotion stops, the price collapses, and everyone who bought in during the hype is left holding a worthless or near-worthless investment.
Red flags: Unsolicited "hot tip" messages pushing a specific stock or crypto token. | Coordinated hype about the same ticker appearing across many accounts at once. | Claims of guaranteed, imminent, massive price gains. | Pressure to buy immediately before "it's too late."
Safety tips: Be skeptical of unsolicited stock or crypto tips promising huge, fast gains. | Research a company's fundamentals independently before buying based on social media hype. | Watch for coordinated promotion of the same ticker across many accounts at once. | Never invest based on pressure to "buy now before it's too late."
Cited source: Investor.gov (U.S. SEC), "Social Media and Stock Tip Scams – Investor Alert," https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins/social-media-stock-scams

## Scam Database: Fake Trading App Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/fake-trading-app-scam.html
Category: Investment Scam
Summary: Victims are convinced to download a fraudulent investment or trading app that shows fabricated, ever-increasing account balances, but withdrawals are blocked or additional "fees" are demanded before any money can be returned.
How it works: A victim is persuaded — often by an online contact or advertisement — to download a trading or investment app that appears professional and fully functional. The app displays a fabricated account balance that climbs steadily as the victim deposits more money, creating the illusion of consistent profit, but when the victim tries to withdraw any funds, the app blocks the transaction or claims additional "taxes," "fees," or "verification deposits" must be paid first, a cycle that continues indefinitely while the deposited money is never actually invested anywhere.
Red flags: An investment app was downloaded outside the official app store or recommended by an online contact. | The account balance grows rapidly and consistently with no losses. | Withdrawal requests are blocked or trigger a demand for an additional fee. | Customer support is unreachable except through the same contact who introduced the app.
Safety tips: Only download trading apps from official app stores, and verify the developer. | Try withdrawing a small amount early to test whether the platform is legitimate. | Be suspicious of any app that requires an additional fee before allowing a withdrawal. | Verify the platform is registered with financial regulators like the SEC or CFTC.
Cited source: FINRA, "Be Alert to Signs of Imposter Investment Scams," https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/be-alert-signs-imposter-investment-scams

## Scam Database: Pig Butchering Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/pig-butchering-scam.html
Category: Investment Scam
Summary: Named for the practice of fattening livestock before slaughter, scammers build a long-term relationship — often starting as a romance or friendship — before gradually persuading the victim to invest increasing amounts into a fake trading platform, ultimately taking everything.
How it works: A scammer initiates contact through a dating app, social media, or even a "wrong number" text, then spends weeks building trust and an emotional connection before mentioning that they, or a relative, have been making significant money trading crypto. They walk the victim through opening a small account on a professional-looking but fake trading platform, showing early "wins" to build confidence, and gradually encourage larger and larger deposits — sometimes urging the victim to take out loans or drain savings — before cutting off contact and disappearing with everything once withdrawals are attempted or the amount invested peaks.
Red flags: A new online contact, sometimes from an unexpected text, builds a personal relationship before mentioning investing. | Early "trades" show quick, easy profits to build confidence. | Increasing pressure to deposit larger amounts, sometimes suggesting loans. | The platform is unfamiliar and was recommended only by this one contact.
Safety tips: Be wary of a new online contact who eventually steers conversation toward an investment opportunity. | Never move funds to a trading platform recommended by someone you've only met online. | Independently verify any platform's registration before depositing money. | Cut off contact and report to authorities as soon as investment pressure begins.
Cited source: FinCEN, "Alert on Prevalent Virtual Currency Investment Scam Commonly Known as 'Pig Butchering'" (FIN-2023-Alert005), September 8, 2023, https://www.fincen.gov/system/files/shared/FinCEN_Alert_Pig_Butchering_FINAL_508c.pdf

## Scam Database: Advance Fee Loan Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/advance-fee-loan-scam.html
Category: Investment Scam
Summary: A "guaranteed approval" loan offer, often targeting people with poor credit, requires an upfront fee for insurance, processing, or collateral before the loan is disbursed — but the loan never actually arrives.
How it works: A lender advertises loans with guaranteed approval regardless of credit history, appealing to people who have been turned down elsewhere. After the victim applies, they're told an upfront payment is required for insurance, processing, or as refundable collateral before the loan can be disbursed, and after that fee is paid the "lender" either invents another fee or disappears entirely, with the promised loan never materializing.
Red flags: Guaranteed loan approval with no credit check. | A required upfront fee before the loan is disbursed. | Pressure to pay via gift card, wire transfer, or prepaid card. | The lender isn't licensed in your state or has no verifiable physical address.
Safety tips: Legitimate lenders deduct fees from the loan amount — they don't require payment upfront. | Be suspicious of any lender who guarantees approval without checking your credit. | Verify a lender is licensed to operate in your state. | Never wire money or use gift cards to pay a loan "fee."
Cited source: Michigan Department of Attorney General, "Advance-Fee Loan Scams," https://www.michigan.gov/consumerprotection/protect-yourself/consumer-alerts/credit/advance-fee-loan-scams

## Scam Database: Fake Online Store Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/fake-online-store-scam.html
Category: Shopping Scam
Summary: A convincing but fraudulent online store, often advertised through social media, offers heavily discounted name-brand products, takes payment, and either ships nothing, a counterfeit, or a completely different item.
How it works: A scammer builds a professional-looking online store, often advertised through targeted social media ads featuring name-brand products at steep discounts, and copies real product photos and descriptions to appear legitimate. After the victim pays, the store either ships nothing at all, a cheap counterfeit, or an entirely different item, and by the time the victim tries to dispute the charge or contact customer service, the store's contact information is fake or unresponsive, and the site may disappear entirely.
Red flags: Prices are dramatically lower than any other retailer for the same brand-name item. | The store was discovered through a social media ad rather than a search or direct visit. | No verifiable physical address or working customer service contact. | Checkout only accepts unusual payment methods like wire transfer or cryptocurrency.
