Safety tips: Search the store name plus "scam" or "reviews" before ordering. | Be cautious of prices that are dramatically lower than anywhere else. | Pay with a credit card rather than a debit card or wire transfer for purchase protection. | Check for a real physical address and working customer service contact.
Cited source: Better Business Bureau, "Think twice before buying from these social media ads," https://www.bbb.org/all/social-media-scams/think-twice-before-buying-from-these-social-media-ads

## Scam Database: Online Marketplace Buyer Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/online-marketplace-buyer-scam.html
Category: Shopping Scam
Summary: A "buyer" on a marketplace app sends a fake payment confirmation screenshot or overpays with a bad check, then asks the seller to ship the item or refund the difference before the payment actually clears.
How it works: A "buyer" contacts a seller on a marketplace app and sends what looks like a payment confirmation screenshot or claims to have overpaid by mistake, then asks the seller to ship the item immediately or refund the "extra" amount before the payment has actually cleared or arrived. Because the seller sees only a fake screenshot or a check that later bounces, they end up shipping merchandise or wiring a refund for money that was never really sent, losing both the item and the "refunded" cash.
Red flags: A buyer sends a payment screenshot instead of you confirming funds in your own account. | The buyer claims to have accidentally overpaid and asks for a refund of the difference. | Payment arrives as a check for more than the asking price. | Pressure to ship or refund quickly before you've verified the payment cleared.
Safety tips: Confirm payment has actually landed in your account, not just a screenshot, before shipping anything. | Be suspicious of any buyer who overpays and asks for a refund of the difference. | Meet locally for cash when possible instead of shipping to unverified buyers. | Use the marketplace's built-in, verified payment system rather than outside apps.
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "The bottom line on fake checks scams," https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2020/02/ftc-bottom-line-fake-checks-scams

## Scam Database: Fake Job Offer Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/fake-job-offer-scam.html
Category: Employment Scam
Summary: A recruiter offers a remote job with little to no interview, then asks the "new hire" to pay for training materials, equipment, or a background check upfront, or to deposit a check and wire back the difference.
How it works: A scammer posts an appealing remote job listing or messages candidates directly, offering a position with little to no real interview process. Once "hired," the victim is asked to pay upfront for training materials, equipment, or a background check, or is sent a check to deposit with instructions to use part of it to purchase equipment from a specific vendor and wire back the remainder — with the original check later bouncing and leaving the victim responsible for the full amount and out any money they wired.
Red flags: A job offer arrives with minimal or no real interview. | A request to pay for training, equipment, or a background check upfront. | Instructions to deposit a check and wire back a portion of it. | Communication happens only through chat or personal email, never a verifiable company account.
Safety tips: Be suspicious of any job offer that skips a real interview process. | Never pay upfront for equipment, training, or a background check. | Research the company independently, including looking for a real office and other employees. | Never deposit a check and wire money back to an "employer."
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Job Scams," https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/job-scams

## Scam Database: Mystery Shopper Check Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/mystery-shopper-check-scam.html
Category: Employment Scam
Summary: A fake mystery shopping job sends the victim a check to deposit, instructing them to keep a "payment" and wire the rest to evaluate a money transfer service — but the original check later bounces, leaving the victim owing the full amount.
How it works: A victim is recruited for a "mystery shopping" assignment that involves evaluating the customer service of a money transfer company, and is mailed a check to deposit into their own bank account. They're instructed to keep a portion as payment and wire the rest through the money transfer service as part of the "evaluation," but the original check is fraudulent and takes days or weeks to bounce — well after the wired money is already gone — leaving the victim's bank holding them responsible for the full amount of the bad check.
Red flags: A "job" that pays by having you deposit a check and wire part of it elsewhere. | The assignment specifically involves evaluating a money transfer or wire service. | The check arrives before any real vetting or interview process. | You're rushed to wire the money quickly after depositing the check.
Safety tips: Be suspicious of any job that pays you by having you deposit and forward a check. | Remember that a bank clearing a check temporarily doesn't mean it won't later be discovered as fraudulent. | Never wire money based on funds from a check you just deposited. | Verify legitimate mystery shopping companies through the Mystery Shopping Professionals Association.
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Mystery Shopping Scams," https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/mystery-shopping-scams

## Scam Database: Package Delivery Text Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/package-delivery-text-scam.html
Category: Delivery Scam
Summary: A text message claims a package couldn't be delivered due to an unpaid fee or incomplete address, with a link to a fake carrier site designed to steal payment card details.
How it works: A text message claims a package couldn't be delivered because of a small unpaid fee or an incomplete address, impersonating a well-known carrier like USPS, FedEx, or UPS, and includes a link to "resolve" the issue. The link leads to a fake site styled to match the real carrier's branding, where the victim is prompted to enter payment card details to pay the small fee, which are then captured and can be used for larger unauthorized charges or sold to other scammers.
Red flags: An unexpected text about a delivery problem or small unpaid fee. | The link goes to a domain that doesn't match the carrier's official website. | Request for full card details to pay a fee of just a dollar or two. | Poor grammar or a generic greeting instead of your name or tracking number.
Safety tips: Track packages directly through the retailer or carrier's official app or website. | Delivery carriers don't typically require a small fee by text message to redeliver a package. | Don't click links in unexpected delivery texts — go to the official site instead. | Forward suspicious delivery texts to 7726 (SPAM) to report them.
Cited source: United States Postal Inspection Service, "Smishing: Package Tracking Text Scams," https://www.uspis.gov/news/scam-article/smishing-package-tracking-text-scams

## Scam Database: Fake Charity / Disaster Relief Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/fake-charity-disaster-relief-scam.html
Category: Charity Scam
Summary: In the wake of a natural disaster or tragedy, fraudulent charities solicit donations through calls, texts, or social media using names deceptively similar to real, established relief organizations.
How it works: In the immediate aftermath of a hurricane, wildfire, mass shooting, or other tragedy, scammers quickly set up fake charities with names deceptively similar to real, well-known relief organizations and solicit donations through cold calls, texts, social media posts, and crowdfunding pages. They rely on the emotional urgency of the moment to bypass the scrutiny a donor might otherwise apply, collecting donations that never reach any actual disaster victims.
Red flags: A charity name is very similar to, but slightly different from, a well-known organization. | High-pressure solicitation for immediate donations right after a disaster. | Vague answers about how the donation will specifically be used. | Requests to donate via gift card, wire transfer, or cash only.
Safety tips: Give directly through a charity's official website rather than through a link in a text or email. | Check a charity's legitimacy on Charity Navigator or the BBB Wise Giving Alliance. | Be wary of high-pressure requests for immediate donations right after a disaster. | Never donate using gift cards or wire transfers.
Cited source: FBI, "Charity and Disaster Fraud," https://www.fbi.gov/how-we-can-help-you/scams-and-safety/common-frauds-and-scams/charity-and-disaster-fraud

## Scam Database: Fake Rental Listing Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/fake-rental-listing-scam.html
Category: Rental Scam
Summary: A rental listing — sometimes copied from a real property that isn't actually for rent — advertises an attractive price and asks for a deposit or first month's rent before the "landlord," who is never available to meet in person, disappears.
How it works: A scammer copies photos and details from a real property listing, or invents one entirely, and posts it online at an attractively low price to generate quick interest. When a prospective renter reaches out, the "landlord" always has an excuse for being unavailable to meet in person — out of the country, deployed, or dealing with a family emergency — and pressures the renter to send a security deposit and first month's rent to hold the unit sight unseen, after which the landlord stops responding and the property often turns out not to be for rent at all.
Red flags: The listed rent is noticeably below market rate for the area. | The landlord is always unavailable to meet in person or show the unit live. | Pressure to send a deposit before viewing the property. | Listing photos match another property listed for sale or rent elsewhere online.
Safety tips: Never pay a deposit before viewing a property in person or via a verified live video call. | Search the listing photos online to check if they've been copied from another listing. | Verify property ownership through public county property records. | Be suspicious of a landlord who is always "out of the country" or unavailable to meet.
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Rental Listing Scams," https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/rental-listing-scams

## Scam Database: Video Call Deepfake Extortion Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/video-call-deepfake-extortion-scam.html
Category: AI Scam
Summary: A stranger video calls you out of nowhere (FaceTime, WhatsApp, or similar), keeps you on briefly while secretly capturing your face, then contacts you later with an AI-manipulated image designed to falsely implicate you in something serious — demanding payment to keep it quiet.
How it works: The scam starts with an unsolicited video call from a number you don't recognize, sometimes with the caller claiming it's a wrong number or pretending to know you. The call is often brief, and the scammer's real goal is just to get a few seconds of your face on camera, which they screen-record. Days or weeks later, using AI image-generation tools, they digitally alter the captured footage into a fabricated image meant to make it look like you did something illegal or deeply shameful. They then contact you demanding immediate, untraceable payment — usually gift cards, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency — threatening to send the fake image to your family, employer, or the police if you don't pay.
Red flags: An unexpected video call from an unknown or international number that ends abruptly. | The caller seems more focused on getting you on camera than having an actual conversation. | Sudden contact later, out of nowhere, with a threatening message and an attached image. | Extreme urgency paired with a demand for immediate, anonymous payment. | The person refuses to slow down, answer questions, or let you verify anything — pure pressure. | The call often opens with a 'wrong number' or 'do I know you?' pretext to get you talking on camera.
Safety tips: Don't accept video calls from unknown or unfamiliar numbers — let them go to voicemail. | Cover your camera when it's not in active, intentional use. | Never send money because of a threat alone — the image is fabricated, not real evidence, and paying almost never makes it stop. | Save screenshots of every message and the threat itself as evidence, then block the sender — don't negotiate or engage further. | If a fabricated intimate image is involved, StopNCII.org (for adults 18+) can help get it removed from participating platforms without ever uploading the image itself. | Report it to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (ic3.gov) and your local police — you are the victim of a crime, not a suspect, and this is a recognized, well-documented scam pattern.
Cited source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), "Malicious Actors Manipulating Photos and Videos to Create Explicit Content and Sextortion Schemes," https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2023/psa230605

## Scam Database: Task-Based "Gamified" Job Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/task-based-gamified-job-scam.html
Category: Employment Scam
Summary: Scammers lure job seekers with texts or WhatsApp messages offering easy remote "tasks" like liking videos or rating products, then trap them in a game-like app that requires crypto deposits to "unlock" fake earnings.
How it works: Victims receive an unsolicited text, WhatsApp, or Telegram message offering a well-paid remote job doing simple repetitive tasks such as liking videos, "optimizing" apps, boosting product listings, or rating products/hotels on an unfamiliar platform. After a short interview-style chat, they're directed to download an app or visit a site where they complete tasks in sets (often 40 per round) and watch a fake balance grow, sometimes receiving a small real payout via PayPal, CashApp, or crypto to build trust. Once invested, the platform introduces "combo" or "lucky" tasks that require the victim to deposit their own money (usually cryptocurrency) to keep their balance positive or to "unlock" the ability to withdraw accumulated earnings; each deposit is followed by a new excuse (a "negative balance," a "tax," or a "withdrawal fee") demanding more money, and the platform ultimately freezes the account or disappears once the victim stops paying.
Red flags: Unsolicited job offer arrives by text, WhatsApp, or Telegram with no formal application or interview process | Job involves simple repetitive tasks (liking videos, rating apps/products/hotels) organized into gamified 'levels' or sets of tasks | You're asked to deposit your own money or cryptocurrency to 'unlock' further tasks, fix a 'negative balance,' or withdraw earnings | Small early payouts are used to build trust before larger deposits are demanded | Pay is unusually high for extremely simple work with no real interview or verifiable employer
Safety tips: Never pay money, crypto, or fees to 'unlock' wages you supposedly already earned 
 require your own money upfront to get paid | Do not respond to unsolicited job texts or messages on WhatsApp/Telegram, especially from unknown numbers with generic greetings | Research the hiring company independently through its official website and legitimate job boards before engaging | Stop immediately if a 'job' asks you to top up a balance in cryptocurrency or claims your account has a negative balance | Report suspected task scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and the FBI's IC3 at ic3.gov, and keep screenshots of messages and transactions as evidence
Cited source: Federal Trade Commission Data Spotlight (Dec. 2024), via Malwarebytes summary: https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/news/2024/12/task-scams-surge-by-400-but-what-are-they ; BBB 2026 Employment Scams Update: https://www.bbb.org/all/scamstudies/jobscams/employment-scams-2026-update

## Scam Database: FTC Official Impersonation Bitcoin ATM Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/ftc-official-impersonation-bitcoin-atm-scam.html
Category: Government Scam
Summary: Scammers are cold-calling consumers claiming to be real, named FTC leaders like Chief Privacy Officer John Krebs or Chairman Andrew Ferguson, falsely accusing them of crimes like money laundering and pressuring them to "resolve" the matter by depositing cash into a Bitcoin ATM.
How it works: A victim receives an unexpected call from someone using the name and title of an actual senior FTC official (such as "agent" John Krebs, or a sitting FTC Commissioner or the Chairman). The caller uses a spoofed caller ID to make the call appear to come from a legitimate government number, and may text a photo of a fake FTC badge or ID card as "proof" of identity. The caller falsely claims the victim is under investigation for money laundering or another serious crime and that their money is at risk. To "fix" the problem or avoid arrest, the caller instructs the victim to withdraw funds and deposit them into a cryptocurrency ATM, or to move money via gift cards or payment apps like Zelle, Cash App, or Venmo, under the pretense of "protecting" it. In reality, the money goes straight to the scammer, and the FTC has no "agents" and never contacts people this way to demand payment.
Red flags: Unexpected call from someone claiming to be an FTC 'agent' or named commissioner (the FTC has no 'agents') | Caller says you're under investigation and must act immediately to avoid arrest or financial loss | Instructions to withdraw money and deposit it into a Bitcoin/cryptocurrency ATM | Caller ID appears to show a government or FTC-linked number (easily spoofed) | A texted photo of a badge or ID card offered as 'proof' of authority | Pressure to move money via gift cards or peer-to-peer payment apps to 'protect' it
Safety tips: Know that the FTC will never call you out of the blue and tell you to move or send money to 'protect' it | Hang up immediately and do not call back any number provided by the caller | Never deposit money into a cryptocurrency ATM, buy gift cards, or send funds via payment apps at the request of an unexpected caller | Independently verify by looking up official contact info yourself rather than trusting caller ID or numbers given during the call | Report the call to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and to DoNotCall.gov
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Scammers are impersonating FTC Chief Privacy Officer John Krebs," Dec. 9, 2025, https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2025/12/scammers-are-impersonating-ftc-chief-privacy-officer-john-krebs

## Scam Database: Fake CAPTCHA "ClickFix" Malware Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/fake-captcha-clickfix-malware-scam.html
Category: Tech Scam
Summary: Scammers plant fake "I'm not a robot" CAPTCHA verification screens on compromised or malicious websites that trick visitors into manually running a hidden malicious command, infecting their own device with password- and data-stealing malware.
How it works: Victims land on a compromised or scam website (often reached via a phishing link, malicious ad, or search result) and are shown a CAPTCHA-style popup that looks like a normal "verify you're human" check. Unlike a real CAPTCHA, which asks you to identify images or type displayed characters, this fake version secretly copies a malicious script to the device's clipboard the moment the user clicks the verification button. It then instructs the victim to "prove they're human" by pressing a keyboard shortcut to open the Run dialog, pasting the clipboard contents, and hitting Enter. Doing so executes a PowerShell or other command-line script that silently downloads and installs information-stealing malware (commonly known as clipboard-hijacking or "ClickFix" attacks), which can harvest saved passwords, browser data, email credentials, and other sensitive information without the victim realizing anything happened.
Red flags: A CAPTCHA or verification screen asks you to press a keyboard shortcut like Windows+R (or Windows+V) instead of simply clicking images or typing displayed text | You're instructed to paste something and hit Enter to 'verify' you're human | The prompt appears on an unfamiliar site, after clicking a link in an unsolicited text/email, or on a page reached through a suspicious search result or ad | The pop-up creates urgency or claims your device needs immediate verification/security confirmation | Any request to run a command, open a system dialog box, or execute code as part of a 'human verification' step
Safety tips: Never follow instructions to press Windows+R, paste content, and press Enter as part of any CAPTCHA or verification process — legitimate CAPTCHAs never require this | If you accidentally pasted and ran a command, disconnect the device from the internet immediately and run a full malware/antivirus scan | Change passwords for email, banking, and other sensitive accounts from a different, uninfected device if you suspect you ran a malicious command | Keep browser and operating system security settings up to date and avoid clicking links or ads from unfamiliar or unsolicited sources | Report suspected fake CAPTCHA or malware pop-ups to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "How to spot a CAPTCHA scam," June 8, 2026, https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/06/how-spot-captcha-scam

## Scam Database: IC3/FBI Recovery Impersonation Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/ic3-fbi-recovery-impersonation-scam.html
Category: Government Scam
Summary: Scammers impersonate FBI and Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) personnel — now using AI deepfake videos and spoofed IC3 websites — to "revictimize" people who already lost money to a scam by falsely offering to recover their funds.
How it works: Criminals target people who have already fallen victim to a scam (or who mention online that they plan to file a fraud report) and pose as FBI agents or IC3 staff reaching out via social media, email, or phone to "help" with the case. They may create fake IC3 social media pages or infiltrate online scam-victim support groups, direct victims to convincing spoofed versions of the real ic3.gov complaint portal, or even show AI-generated deepfake videos of senior FBI officials to build credibility. The scammer then claims funds have been recovered or offers "assistance" recovering lost money, but the real goal is to harvest additional personal and financial information or extract upfront "recovery fees," compounding the victim's original loss.
Red flags: Being contacted out of the blue by someone claiming to be FBI/IC3 staff after a prior scam or online complaint | Any request for payment, gift cards, or cryptocurrency to "recover" lost funds | Social media profiles or pages claiming to represent IC3 or offering fund recovery services | Being directed to a website that looks like ic3.gov but arrived via a link in a message rather than typed directly | Video calls or recordings featuring FBI officials that were unsolicited or shared via social media DM | Pressure to act quickly or share sensitive personal/financial details to 'verify' a recovered case
Safety tips: Only file or check complaints at the official site by typing www.ic3.gov directly into your browser, never via a link sent to you | Know that the IC3 will never ask for payment, gift cards, or crypto to recover lost funds, nor refer you to a company that charges recovery fees | Do not share personal or financial information with anyone you've only met online or by phone, even if they claim to be law enforcement | Verify any claimed FBI contact by calling your local FBI field office directly using a number you look up independently | Be skeptical of unsolicited videos of officials on social media, which can be AI-generated deepfakes | If you're a repeat contact target after reporting a scam, treat any follow-up 'recovery' outreach as highly suspicious and report it to IC3
Cited source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), Public Service Announcement PSA260720, "FBI Warns of Scammers Impersonating the IC3" - https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260720

## Scam Database: Fake "Relief Check" Phishing Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/fake-relief-check-phishing-scam.html
Category: Government Scam
Summary: Scammers are calling, texting, and emailing people claiming they have an unclaimed "relief check" worth thousands of dollars waiting for them, directing victims to phishing sites to "search their name" and steal personal and financial data.
How it works: Victims receive a call, voicemail, or text — often from someone identifying himself as "Dan" — claiming government records show a specific dollar amount (commonly cited around $5,286) is waiting for them in a relief check tied to "past relief programs or federal assistance payments." The message urges the victim to visit a website such as myreliefcheck.com or myreliefclaim.com to search their name and "collect it before it's returned." The site is not affiliated with any real government agency; instead, it prompts victims to enter personal identifying information and banking details to "claim" the payment. Handing over this data exposes victims to identity theft, drained bank accounts, and continued follow-up contact from scammers via additional calls, texts, or emails attempting to extract more money or information. The scam has been amplified by news coverage of the recent federal government shutdown, which scammers exploit to make the "relief payment" premise feel more plausible.
Red flags: Unsolicited call, voicemail, or text claiming you have an unclaimed government relief check waiting | You're told to visit a third-party website (not a .gov domain) and "search your name" to claim money | A vague personal name like "Dan" is used with no verifiable agency affiliation | Urgency pressure to act "before it's returned" | Requests for personal identifying information or bank details to "release" a payment | Ties the offer to current news events like a government shutdown or old COVID-era relief programs
Safety tips: Never click links in unsolicited texts, emails, or voicemails about unclaimed government money | Verify any claimed government payment directly through official .gov websites or by calling the agency using a number you look up independently | Do not enter personal or banking information on websites referenced in unsolicited calls or texts | Hang up on robocalls or voicemails claiming to be from government relief programs and do not call back the number provided | Report suspicious messages to the BBB Scam Tracker, the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov, and your phone carrier
Cited source: Better Business Bureau, "BBB Scam Alert: Fake relief check phone calls claim you have money waiting" - https://www.bbb.org/all/consumer/scam/fake-relief-check-scam

## Scam Database: Gold Bar & Bulk Cash Courier Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/gold-bar-bulk-cash-courier-scam.html
Category: Government Scam
Summary: Scammers impersonating grandchildren, government agents, or tech support convince mostly elderly victims to withdraw cash or buy gold bars, then send an in-person courier to physically collect the loot from the victim's home.
How it works: A fraudster first gains a victim's trust through a grandparent-emergency call, a government/law-enforcement impersonation call, or a tech-support pop-up, convincing the victim their money is at risk or a relative is in trouble. Instead of asking for a wire transfer or gift cards, the scammer instructs the victim to withdraw large amounts of cash or, increasingly, to purchase physical gold bars from a dealer "to protect the funds." The criminal then arranges for a courier, sometimes an unwitting rideshare driver and sometimes a knowing accomplice, to come to the victim's home or a nearby meeting point to physically pick up the cash or gold. To make the handoff seem legitimate, the scammer often gives the victim a verification "code," "password," or "serial number" that the courier must recite before the victim hands over the money or gold.
Red flags: A caller you don't know instructs you to withdraw cash or buy gold bars and hand them to a stranger who comes to your door | You're told to give a courier a special code, password, or serial number to verify who should receive the money | Urgent claims that a family member is in legal trouble, your accounts are compromised, or the government needs you to move your money to "protect" it | Instructions to keep the transaction secret from other family members or bank staff | Pressure to act immediately with no time to verify the story independently
Safety tips: Never give cash, gold, or valuables to a courier sent by someone who contacted you unsolicited by phone, email, or pop-up | Independently verify any claim of a relative's emergency or government/legal trouble by calling them or the agency directly using a number you look up yourself | Real government agencies (FBI, IRS, Social Security, etc.) will never ask you to buy gold bars or hand cash to a courier | Talk to a trusted family member or your bank before withdrawing large sums or buying precious metals under pressure | Report suspected courier pickup scams to the FBI's IC3.gov and local police immediately, even if you're embarrassed
Cited source: FBI Boston Division, "FBI Boston Warns of Increase in Gold Bar and Bulk Cash Courier Scams," September 22, 2025, https://www.fbi.gov/contact-us/field-offices/boston/news/fbi-boston-warns-of-increase-in-gold-bar-and-bulk-cash-courier-scams

## Scam Database: Deepfake Job Candidate / Fake AI Employee Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/deepfake-job-candidate-fake-ai-employee-scam.html
Category: AI Scam
Summary: Scammers, many linked to North Korean state-sponsored operations, use AI deepfake video/audio, stolen identities, and ChatGPT-polished resumes to get hired into remote jobs, then use the position to steal company data, plant malware, or funnel salary payments overseas.
How it works: A fraudster builds a fake professional identity using a stolen or synthetic Social Security number, an AI-generated or "face-swapped" profile photo, and an AI-polished resume, then applies for legitimate remote tech or IT jobs. During video interviews, the applicant uses real-time deepfake face-swap and voice-cloning software (sometimes with a live "coach" typing answers) to appear as a different, more qualified or more "American-sounding" person than they really are. Once hired, the fake employee (in many documented cases tied to North Korean IT worker schemes) receives a company laptop, often routed to a US-based "laptop farm," logs in via VPN, and either collects a legitimate salary that gets funneled overseas to fund weapons programs, or uses insider access to exfiltrate sensitive data, install malware, or extort the employer after termination. Security researchers report the fraud has scaled dramatically, with some hiring managers estimating a huge share of remote-job applicants are now fake AI-generated candidates.
Red flags: Candidate's lip movements, blinking, or facial edges look slightly out of sync or glitchy during video calls, especially at profile angles or with rapid head movement | Applicant refuses to turn on camera for parts of the interview or gives excuses for poor video/audio quality | Resume, LinkedIn history, and interview answers feel AI-polished but generic, or the candidate's home address, bank routing details, and shipping address for equipment don't match | Candidate insists on having a company laptop shipped to an address that turns out to be a freight-forwarding or 'laptop farm' location rather than their stated home | Multiple candidates for different job postings share similar resume phrasing, photos, or reference contacts | New hire immediately requests VPN access, remote log-in tools, or asks to reroute the equipment shortly after onboarding
Safety tips: Verify identity documents in person or via a live, unscripted video check where you ask the candidate to turn their head to the side or perform an unscripted action a deepfake would struggle to replicate | Cross-check the shipping address for company equipment against the candidate's stated home address and reject freight-forwarding or unfamiliar third-party addresses | Use identity-verification and deepfake-detection tools during high-stakes remote hiring for sensitive IT or data-access roles | Limit new remote hires' system access and monitor for anomalous VPN logins, unusual work hours, or connections from unexpected countries during onboarding | Train HR and hiring managers to recognize red flags of AI-generated resumes, synthetic photos, and coached video interviews, and report suspected cases to the FBI/IC3
Cited source: FBI/IC3 Advisory "North Korean IT Workers Conducting Data Extortion" (ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250123); NYSBA "Addressing the Threat of Fake Job Candidates" (nysba.org, May 2026); CNBC "Fake job seekers use AI to interview for remote jobs" (April 8, 2025)

## Scam Database: AI-Cloned Fake Vehicle Dealership Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/ai-cloned-fake-vehicle-dealership-scam.html
Category: Shopping Scam
Summary: Scammers use AI tools to clone real dealership websites or build entirely fake auto/RV dealership sites and Facebook ad campaigns, then convince buyers to wire large sums for vehicles that don't exist.
How it works: Fraudsters build convincing dealership websites using AI-generated or AI-altered photos, sometimes cloning an existing legitimate dealer's name, staff listings, and inventory, or inventing a fake company entirely. They advertise heavily on Facebook and other social platforms, often listing a real-looking business address that turns out to be an empty lot or unrelated location. When a buyer inquires, scammers engage in days- or weeks-long conversations to build trust and answer questions convincingly before pressuring the victim to wire money for a vehicle that was never actually for sale, at which point communication stops and the money is gone. Risk-management researchers have identified over a hundred of these "dealership cloning" sites impersonating active or defunct dealers.
Red flags: Dealership's website photos look slightly off, too polished, or have inconsistent details when zoomed in (AI-altered images) | Seller insists on a wire transfer before you can see the vehicle in person or meet at the dealership | Listed business address turns out to be a parking lot, empty building, or unrelated business when checked on Google Maps | Misspelled business name or slight variations from a real, known dealership name | Heavy pressure to move quickly on a 'too good to be true' price advertised via a Facebook or social media ad | Communication happens only by text/chat/email with no way to verify a real, listed phone number
Safety tips: Independently look up the dealership's phone number and address rather than using contact info from the ad or website, and call to verify the vehicle and transaction directly | Visit the dealership in person or verify its physical existence via Google Street View before wiring any funds | Never wire money for a vehicle sight-unseen; use verifiable, traceable payment methods and complete the purchase at a legitimate, confirmed dealership location | Reverse-image-search listing photos to check if they've been copied or AI-altered from another source | Be suspicious of deals advertised primarily through social media ads offering prices well below market value
Cited source: Auto Finance News, autofinancenews.net/allposts/risk-management/ai-cloning-scam-impersonates-dealerships-with-fake-websites/; Autoblog, autoblog.com/news/ai-is-making-fake-car-dealerships-look-real-and-its-costing-buyers-thousands; WAFB, wafb.com/2026/07/22/bbb-warns-ai-powered-rv-dealer-scam-targeting-facebook-users/

## Scam Database: Spoofed IC3/FBI Fraud-Reporting Website Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/spoofed-ic3-fbi-fraud-reporting-website-scam.html
Category: Government Scam
Summary: Criminals are building near-exact clones of the FBI's official Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3.gov) website to steal personal and financial data from people who are trying to report a scam they were already victimized by.
How it works: Scam victims searching online for how to report fraud, or who click a "sponsored" search ad, social media post, or link shared in a scam-recovery group, land on a fake site built to look like the real IC3.gov complaint portal, often using a domain with slight misspellings or a different top-level domain. The cloned page mimics the FBI seal, banner text, and even the genuine site's own warning about impersonators, then presents a "complaint form" that harvests names, addresses, emails, phone numbers, and banking details. Some versions follow up by emailing a fake confirmation of the "report," or by having a scammer posing as IC3/FBI personnel contact the victim on messaging apps to offer fund "recovery," pushing them toward a second round of financial loss.
Red flags: Arriving at 'ic3' or 'FBI' report sites through a search ad, social media post, or a link someone else sent rather than typing the address yourself | URL that is close to but not exactly www.ic3.gov (extra words, hyphens, or a non-.gov ending) | Being contacted afterward by someone claiming to be FBI/IC3 staff offering to help recover money you reported losing | Low-quality graphics, odd phrasing, or a complaint form asking for banking log-in details or payment before it will 'process' your report
Safety tips: Type www.ic3.gov directly into your browser's address bar instead of searching for it, and never click 'sponsored' search results | Double-check that the URL ends in .gov and reads exactly www.ic3.gov before entering any information | Never send money or provide banking passwords to anyone contacting you about a complaint you filed or offering to recover lost funds | If you suspect you used a spoofed site, monitor your accounts, place a fraud alert with credit bureaus, and file a genuine report directly on ic3.gov
Cited source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center, PSA "Threat Actors Spoofing the FBI IC3 Website for Possible Malicious Activity," https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250919

## Scam Database: "Ghost Tapping" Contactless Payment Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/ghost-tapping-contactless-payment-scam.html
Category: Shopping Scam
Summary: Scammers exploit NFC "tap-to-pay" technology to charge victims' cards or phones without authorization, often by posing as vendors or charity collectors at crowded markets, fairs, and festivals.
How it works: "Ghost tapping" abuses Near Field Communication (NFC), the wireless technology that lets contactless cards and mobile wallets exchange payment data at very close range. In one version, a fraudster poses as a market vendor, food stall, or charity fundraiser who only accepts tap-to-pay, approaches the victim closely, and uses an altered or portable card reader to charge far more than the agreed amount while rushing the victim so they don't check the terminal screen or get a receipt. In another version, criminals use a hidden RFID/NFC reader to "bump" or get within a couple of inches of an unprotected card or phone in a crowd (subway, concert, festival) and skim payment credentials, sometimes loading them into a relay app on another phone to make fraudulent purchases elsewhere. Victims often don't notice anything happened until small, repeated unauthorized charges appear on their statements later.
Red flags: A vendor, fundraiser, or seller who insists on tap-to-pay only and refuses cash or chip/PIN alternatives | The person rushes you through the transaction, blocks your view of the card reader screen, or doesn't give you a receipt | Someone stands unusually close to you or bumps into you in a crowded place like a fair, festival, or public transit | Small, unfamiliar charges appear on your card or digital wallet statement after visiting a crowded event | A door-to-door 'charity' collector asks for tap-to-pay donations without proper identification or paperwork
Safety tips: Keep cards and NFC-enabled phones in an RFID-blocking wallet or sleeve when not actively paying | Always glance at the terminal screen to confirm the merchant name and exact amount before tapping | Set up real-time transaction alerts with your bank or card issuer so you're notified of every charge immediately | Avoid storing more cards than necessary in mobile wallet apps to limit exposure if a device is compromised | Regularly review bank and card statements for small, unrecognized charges, especially after crowded public events | Verify charity collectors' identification and prefer donating directly through an organization's official website instead of an in-person tap-to-pay request
Cited source: Better Business Bureau / Fox News, "How to protect yourself from ghost-tapping payment card scams nationwide," https://www.foxnews.com/tech/ghost-tapping-scam-targets-tap-to-pay-users

## Scam Database: Fake VPN App Malware Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/fake-vpn-app-malware-scam.html
Category: Tech Scam
Summary: Cybercriminals are distributing malicious apps and browser extensions disguised as popular VPN services to secretly install info-stealing and banking malware on victims' devices.
How it works: Scammers build convincing lookalike VPN apps or browser extensions that impersonate well-known, trusted VPN brands, then distribute them through official app stores, ads, and other platforms using misleading marketing, sexually suggestive ads, or trending geopolitical headlines to drive downloads. Once a victim installs the fake VPN, instead of adding privacy protection it does the opposite: it delivers malware payloads such as info-stealers, remote access trojans (RATs), and banking trojans. These payloads exfiltrate sensitive data including browsing history, private messages, financial credentials, and cryptocurrency wallet information, and can give attackers remote access to the device.
Red flags: A 'VPN' app or extension promising complete anonymity or unusually broad privacy claims | Free VPN apps that request excessive permissions, such as access to contacts, messages, or storage | Apps found outside official stores, or promoted via aggressive/suggestive ads or sensational geopolitical headlines | Slight misspellings or subtle URL/branding differences from the real VPN provider's official app or website | Unverified developer names or a fraudulent 'security firm' publishing multiple similar VPN apps
Safety tips: Only download VPN apps from official app stores and the provider's verified official domain, double-checking for misspellings | Avoid free VPN services that request permissions unrelated to VPN functionality, like access to contacts or messages | Research the VPN provider's reputation and reviews before installing, and prefer well-established, paid providers with transparent privacy policies | Enable enhanced protection features (e.g., Chrome's Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection) that warn against malicious sites and fraudulent downloads | Remember a VPN masks your IP address but does not guarantee total anonymity or safety—treat any app claiming otherwise with skepticism
Cited source: Google Safety & Security Blog, "Google's November 2025 frauds and scams advisory," https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/safety-security/fraud-and-scams-advisory-november-2025/; Forbes, https://www.forbes.com/sites/daveywinder/2025/11/11/google-issues-critical-vpn-threat-warning-for-billions-of-users/

## Scam Database: SpyLoan Predatory Loan App Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/spyloan-predatory-loan-app-scam.html
Category: Tech Scam
Summary: Malicious "instant loan" apps on Google Play and the Apple App Store lure people with promises of quick cash, then harvest contacts, photos, and messages from their phones to blackmail and harass them into paying inflated fees.
How it works: Scammers publish seemingly legitimate personal-loan or finance apps on official app stores or push them through social media ads and SMS links. During setup, the app demands excessive permissions unrelated to lending, such as access to contacts, SMS history, photos, camera, and call logs. Once a "loan" is issued (often smaller than promised and with hidden fees or predatory interest), the operators use the stolen personal data to harass, publicly shame, or threaten the victim and people in their contact list in order to pressure repayment at inflated rates, turning a loan request into extortion and financial exploitation.
Red flags: App requests permissions with no clear connection to lending, such as contacts, photos, SMS, or camera access | Loan is advertised as instant, no-credit-check, with minimal documentation required | App was discovered via a social media ad or unsolicited text link rather than a trusted financial institution | Fees, interest rates, or repayment terms change after the loan is disbursed | Threats to contact or expose the borrower's friends/family if payment is late
Safety tips: Only download lending or finance apps from well-established, verified financial institutions and check developer legitimacy before installing | Review and deny any permission requests (contacts, photos, SMS, camera) that are not essential to a loan app's function | Verify any lender's registration with your country's financial regulator before submitting personal or banking information | Uninstall suspicious loan apps immediately, revoke their permissions, and change any passwords or PINs shared with the app | Report predatory or extortionate loan apps to the app store and to consumer protection agencies like the FTC or BBB
Cited source: Check Point Research Blog, "Malicious Loan App Removed from iOS and Google Play App Store Posed Severe Risks to Users," Sept. 9, 2025, https://blog.checkpoint.com/research/malicious-loan-app-removed-from-ios-and-google-play-app-store-posed-severe-risks-to-users/; corroborated by McAfee Labs Blog (Nov. 25, 2024) and Google's November 2025 Frauds and Scams Advisory (blog.google)

## Scam Database: Fake Loan Approval/Follow-Up Text Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/fake-loan-approval-follow-up-text-scam.html
Category: Phone Scam
Summary: Scammers send unsolicited texts claiming to "follow up" on a large loan application (often $10,000) that the recipient never submitted, pressuring them to click a link or reply to "cancel" it and steal personal data instead.
How it works: Victims receive an out-of-the-blue text saying they've been preapproved for a loan or that representatives are following up on a loan application, even though they never applied. The message creates false urgency with phrases like "this is the last step" or asks the recipient to reply YES to confirm or NO to cancel, which merely confirms the number is active. If the person calls the listed number or clicks the link, the "lender" asks for a Social Security number or bank account number to "finish" the application. In reality there is no loan and no lender; the goal is to harvest personal information for identity theft or to extract fees, and the operation frequently rotates through invented company names to dodge spam filters and negative reviews.
Red flags: An unsolicited text about a loan you never applied for | Promises of guaranteed pre-approval for a large, specific dollar amount | Requests for a Social Security number or bank account number to "complete" an application | Urgency language like "this is the last step" or instructions to reply YES/NO | A callback number embedded in the text rather than a verifiable company website | Company name that has no findable, verifiable lending license or history
Safety tips: Don't reply to or click links in unsolicited loan texts \u2014 delete them | Never give a Social Security number or bank account number in response to an unexpected text | Forward suspicious texts to 7726 (SPAM) and report them at ReportFraud.ftc.gov | Verify any loan offer independently by contacting a lender through its official, verified website or phone number, not the one in the text | Talk to a trusted friend or family member before responding if you're unsure | If you already shared personal information, visit IdentityTheft.gov for recovery steps
Cited source: Federal Trade Commission, Consumer Alert "Can you spot a fake loan text scam?" (Jan. 20, 2026), consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/01/can-you-spot-fake-loan-text-scam

## Scam Database: Fake Toll Road Text Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/fake-toll-road-text-scam.html
Category: Government Scam
Summary: Scammers send text messages impersonating toll agencies like E-ZPass, SunPass, FasTrak, and TxTag, claiming the recipient owes money for an unpaid toll and must pay immediately via a malicious link.
How it works: Victims receive an unsolicited SMS or iMessage claiming they have an outstanding toll balance or violation on a real regional toll system, often threatening late fees, suspended registration, or legal action if they don't pay right away. The message includes a link to a spoofed website that closely mimics the real toll agency's site, where victims are prompted to "log in" or enter payment details, Social Security numbers, or other personal data to resolve the supposed debt. Instead of paying a toll, victims hand their credit card numbers and personal information directly to criminals, who can then make fraudulent charges or commit identity theft. The scam has become the leading driver of a broader surge in government-impersonation fraud reported to the FTC.
Red flags: Unexpected text about an unpaid toll, especially if you don't use that toll road or an EZ-Pass/SunPass/FasTrak/TxTag account | Urgent, high-pressure language like 'final notice' or threats of late fees, fines, or legal action for not paying immediately | A link in the text rather than being told to log into the toll agency's official app or website directly | Generic greetings like 'Dear Customer' instead of your name or actual account/license plate details | Requests for payment via gift cards, cryptocurrency, or other non-standard payment methods | Misspellings, odd phrasing, or a sender number/domain that doesn't match the toll agency's official contact information
Safety tips: Don't click links in unsolicited toll-payment texts; go directly to the toll agency's official website or app by typing the address yourself | Check your actual toll account balance by logging in independently or calling the agency's verified customer service number | Delete or report suspicious toll texts (forward to 7726/SPAM) and report them to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov | Never enter your Social Security number, full credit card number, or account login through a link sent via text | Monitor your bank and credit card statements for unauthorized charges if you've already clicked a suspicious toll link, and consider freezing your credit
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "New trends in reports of imposter scams," https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/05/new-trends-reports-imposter-scams

## Scam Database: Fake Heavy Equipment & Vehicle Dealer Website Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/fake-heavy-equipment-vehicle-dealer-website-scam.html
Category: Shopping Scam
Summary: Scammers clone or impersonate real heavy equipment, farm machinery, and vehicle dealerships with convincing fake websites and Marketplace ads, luring buyers with below-market prices and then vanishing after victims wire large payments.
How it works: Fraudsters build a professional-looking website (or Facebook Marketplace ad) that copies the name, logo, photos, and even fabricated regulatory license numbers of a real, often long-established or now-closed, equipment or vehicle dealership. They list tractors, excavators, skid steers, trucks, or cars at prices noticeably below market value to create urgency. When a buyer inquires, the "seller" provides wiring or ACH instructions, sometimes sending a fake shipping confirmation, invoice, or even a real-looking VIN, and pressures the buyer to pay quickly, often before ever seeing the equipment in person. Once payment clears, the scammers cut off phone and email contact, the equipment never arrives, and the buyer discovers the impersonated business had no knowledge of the sale. In some cases scammers use compromised servers to run dozens of similar fake dealer sites simultaneously, each claiming to be based in a different U.S. region, and some have even tried filing false business update requests with the BBB to shift blame onto uninvolved local companies.
Red flags: Price is well below market value for the make, model, or equipment type | Seller insists on wire transfer or ACH payment and refuses other secure payment methods | Seller avoids phone calls or video verification and won't allow an in-person inspection before payment | Website or ad was created very recently, or contact information doesn't match the real dealership's official listing | Seller becomes unreachable (disconnected phone, bounced email) immediately after payment is sent | Listing photos and descriptions appear identical across multiple unrelated 'dealer' websites
Safety tips: Research the business at BBB.org or call your local BBB before sending any money | Contact the real dealership directly using a phone number or website you find independently, not one provided in the ad | Never wire money or use ACH transfer to purchase equipment or vehicles from a seller you haven't verified in person | Insist on an in-person inspection or a live video walkthrough of the actual item before paying anything | Check how recently the seller's website domain was registered using a WHOIS lookup | Verify serial numbers or VINs directly with the manufacturer or DMV rather than trusting documents the seller provides
Cited source: Better Business Bureau, "BBB Study: Impostor scammers target consumers, businesses and BBB," https://www.bbb.org/article/news-releases/31436-bbb-study-watch-out-for-vehicle-and-equipment-impostor-scams; and "BBB Scam Alert: BBB warns of online equipment scam, impersonating Missouri dealer," https://www.bbb.org/article/scams/32122-bbb-warns-of-online-equipment-scam-impersonating-missouri-dealer

## Scam Database: SEO Poisoning Bank Account Takeover Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/seo-poisoning-bank-account-takeover-scam.html
Category: Phone Scam
Summary: Criminals buy fake search-engine ads or build lookalike phishing sites that outrank real bank, payroll, and health savings account login pages, then trick victims into handing over passwords and one-time codes to drain their accounts.
How it works: Scammers use a technique called "SEO poisoning," purchasing search ads or optimizing fraudulent pages so they appear above or alongside a real financial institution's website when someone searches for their bank's login or customer support number. Victims click the fake ad or link, land on a convincing clone of the real site or speak to a fake "support" agent, and are manipulated through social engineering (calls, texts, emails, or fraudulent websites) into revealing login credentials, multi-factor authentication codes, or one-time passcodes. Once criminals gain account access, they quickly wire funds to other criminal-controlled accounts, many linked to cryptocurrency wallets, making the money extremely difficult to recover. The scheme targets not just personal bank accounts but also business accounts, payroll systems, and health savings accounts.
Red flags: An unsolicited call, text, or email from someone claiming to be your bank's support staff asking you to verify login credentials, MFA codes, or OTPs | Search results or ads for your bank's 'customer service number' or login page that look slightly different from the official URL | Being asked to read back a one-time passcode or multi-factor authentication code to 'verify your identity' | Urgent pressure to act immediately on a supposed account problem, fraud alert, or login issue | A support number found via a search engine ad rather than the number printed on your card or official bank statement
Safety tips: Never provide login credentials, passwords, or one-time passcodes to anyone who contacts you, even if they claim to be from your bank | Navigate directly to your financial institution's website by typing the known URL yourself rather than clicking search ads or links | If a caller claims to be from your bank, hang up and call back using the number on the back of your card or official statement | Enable strong, unique passwords and multi-factor authentication, and avoid posting personal details online that could help attackers guess security answers | Report suspected account takeover attempts to your financial institution immediately and file a complaint with IC3.gov using the keywords 'account takeover' or 'SEO poisoning'
Cited source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), Public Service Announcement I-112525-PSA, https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA251125

## Scam Database: FTC Impersonator Fake Employee ID Refund Recovery Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/ftc-impersonator-fake-employee-id-refund-recovery-scam.html
Category: Government Scam
Summary: Scammers text or WhatsApp victims claiming to be FTC "agents" who can help recover money lost in a previous scam, sending a photo of a fake employee badge/ID to seem legitimate before stealing money or financial data.
How it works: Fraudsters contact people—often those who already lost money to an earlier scam or filed a fraud report—via text message or a messaging app like WhatsApp, claiming to be an FTC employee or "agent" who can help recover their prior losses. To build trust, the scammer sends a photo of what looks like an official government employee ID card and badge, all of which are fabricated. Once the victim is convinced, the scammer asks them to pay a fee, move money into an account the scammer controls, or hand over bank account or Social Security information supposedly needed to process the "refund." In reality the FTC has no such recovery agents, never initiates contact this way, and the victim's money or data is simply stolen.
Red flags: Contact by text message or WhatsApp from someone claiming to be an FTC employee or 'agent' | Being sent a photo of an employee ID or badge as 'proof' of identity | Any claim that a government employee can personally help recover money lost in a past scam | Requests to pay a fee, move money to a specified account, or share bank/Social Security details to receive a refund | Urgency or pressure to act quickly to 'secure' recovered funds
Safety tips: Remember a real FTC employee will never contact you by text or messaging app to discuss a case or refund | Know that the FTC never texts photos of employee IDs or badges to 'verify' identity | Never pay a fee, wire money, or send crypto/gift cards to anyone claiming they can recover scam losses | Do not share bank account numbers or Social Security numbers with unsolicited contacts claiming to be government officials | Verify by going directly to official FTC.gov contact channels rather than replying to the text or calling numbers it provides
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "A real FTC employee won't text you their photo ID to 'verify' their identity," https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/06/real-ftc-employee-wont-text-you-their-photo-id-verify-their-identity

## Scam Database: Refund and Recovery "Sucker List" Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/refund-and-recovery-sucker-list-scam.html
Category: Government Scam
Summary: Scammers buy and sell lists of people who were previously defrauded, then pose as government agencies, law firms, or consumer groups offering to recover the victim's lost money for an upfront fee — draining them a second time.
How it works: After someone falls for an initial scam, their contact details and information about how they were scammed often end up on a "sucker list" that fraud rings buy and sell. A new scammer then calls, emails, texts, messages on social media, or mails a letter claiming they can help recover the money, prize, or merchandise the person lost. They may claim to be from a federal agency like the FTC, a consumer advocacy group, a law firm, or even the original scammy company offering refunds to "dissatisfied customers." Because they already know details of the original fraud, their pitch sounds credible. Before "releasing" the recovered funds, they ask the victim to pay an upfront "retainer fee," "processing fee," "administrative charge," "tax," or "shipping and handling charge," or to hand over a Social Security number or bank/debit account information — which the scammer then uses to steal money or commit identity theft. The FTC also warns scammers are now using AI to make these pitches look and sound more legitimate.
Red flags: Someone contacts you out of the blue claiming they can recover money you lost to a past scam | You're asked to pay any kind of upfront fee, 'tax,' or 'processing charge' before receiving a promised refund | The caller already knows details about a prior scam you experienced and uses that to build trust | They ask for your Social Security number, bank account, or other financial/personal information to 'process' the refund | They pressure you to pay via cash, gift cards, cryptocurrency, or wire transfer | They claim to guarantee they can get your name 'to the top of a list' for reimbursement
Safety tips: Never pay an upfront fee or give financial/personal information to get a refund "no legitimate government agency or company requires this | If someone contacts you claiming to be from a government agency or law firm about a past scam, independently look up and call that organization directly rather than using contact info they provide | Search the organization's name online along with words like 'complaint,' 'scam,' or 'review' before engaging further | Be skeptical of any unsolicited call, text, email, or social media message referencing a scam you previously fell for | Avoid searching online for 'scam recovery' or similar help services, as this can lead directly to more recovery scammers | Report suspected refund/recovery scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov
Cited source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Refund and Recovery Scams," https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/refund-and-recovery-scams

## Scam Database: Financial Institution Support Impersonation Account Takeover Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/financial-institution-support-impersonation-account-takeover-scam.html
Category: Phone Scam
Summary: The FBI warns that criminals are impersonating banks, payroll providers, and health savings account (HSA) administrators to trick people into handing over login credentials and one-time passcodes, then draining or hijacking the accounts.
How it works: Criminals pose as a financial institution's support staff or replicate its website, then use texts, phone calls, emails, or fraudulent lookalike websites to manipulate the account holder into giving up login credentials, multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes, or one-time passcodes (OTPs). Once the criminal has this information, they log into the victim's actual online banking, payroll, or health savings account and use the access to steal funds, redirect paychecks, or otherwise move money out of the victim's control. The scheme targets individuals as well as businesses and organizations of all sizes across sectors, not just personal bank customers.
Red flags: Unsolicited text, call, or email claiming to be from your bank, payroll provider, or HSA administrator asking you to verify your login or share a code | A request for your multi-factor authentication code or one-time passcode over the phone or via text/email | Being directed to click a link or download software to 'resolve' an account issue rather than logging in directly through the official app or website | A sense of urgency pushing you to act immediately to 'secure' or 'verify' your account | Slight misspellings or odd URLs in a bank/payroll website link sent to you
Safety tips: Never share your login credentials, MFA codes, or one-time passcodes with anyone who contacts you, even if they claim to be from your bank or employer | Contact your financial institution, payroll provider, or HSA administrator directly using a phone number or website you look up yourself, not one provided in the suspicious message | If you suspect your account was accessed, contact your financial institution immediately to request a recall or reversal and a Hold Harmless Letter, and reset all potentially exposed credentials and passwords, including on other sites where you reused them | Report suspected account takeover fraud to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov, including the words 'Account Takeover' or 'SEO poisoning' in the description, and notify the impersonated company so it can warn others
Cited source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), PSA I-112525-PSA, https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA251125

## Scam Database: Health Insurer + Chinese Law Enforcement Impersonation Extortion Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/health-insurer-chinese-law-enforcement-impersonation-extortion-scam.html
Category: Government Scam
Summary: The FBI warns that criminals are targeting Chinese-speaking residents of the U.S. by impersonating health insurance claims departments and then handing the call off to fake Chinese police who threaten extradition unless the victim pays "bail."
How it works: According to an FBI/IC3 public service announcement, targeted individuals receive a call from a spoofed telephone number belonging to a legitimate U.S. health insurance provider's claims department, conducted in Chinese, asking about recent insurance claims for alleged surgical procedures; the criminal then shows the recipient fraudulent invoices on screen via video communication software and demands payment. If the recipient denies filing the claim, the criminal transfers them to someone posing as Chinese law enforcement, who asks for personal identifying information, threatens extradition or foreign prosecution, and demands a large payment for bail, and may instruct the victim to download video communication software and stay connected for 24-hour "surveillance."
Red flags: An unsolicited call in Chinese claiming to be from a health insurer's claims department about a surgery you never had | Being shown invoices over video call and pressured to pay immediately | A second caller claiming to be Chinese police who demands personal ID information and a 'bail' payment | Instructions to download video software and stay connected around the clock for 'surveillance' | Threats of extradition or foreign prosecution over an insurance dispute
Safety tips: Independently verify any health insurance claim by using the phone number or website printed on your insurance card, not one given by the caller | Do not share personal information, including health insurance account logins, with an unsolicited caller | Never wire money or pay 'bail' to anyone who calls you, especially foreign law enforcement claiming jurisdiction over a US resident | Do not install video communication software or allow anyone to maintain live video access to your device | Hang up and report the call to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) with any phone numbers, names, or transaction details
Cited source: FBI/IC3, https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA251113

## Scam Database: Virtual Casting Call Text Scam

Source: https://scampedia.net/scams/virtual-casting-call-text-scam.html
Category: Employment Scam
Summary: Scammers send unsolicited texts posing as talent scouts offering movie or TV auditions, then pressure victims into paying for fake photo shoots or acting classes.
How it works: Victims receive an unexpected text message from a supposed "talent scout" claiming they've been selected for a virtual audition tied to a well-known movie or television show. The message asks if the recipient is available for a casting call they never actually signed up for. Anyone who responds may be routed into a "virtual audition" that turns out to be a high-pressure sales pitch to enroll in bogus paid photo shoots or fake acting classes, with the scammer eventually asking for payment or bank information as a supposed condition of participating in the casting.
Red flags: An unexpected text about an audition or casting call you never applied for | Being asked to pay for test shoots, headshots, or to 'secure your spot' before any job is confirmed | High-pressure sales pitch during a so-called virtual audition | Requests for bank information tied to participating in a casting call | Name-dropping specific popular movies or shows to seem credible
Safety tips: Never respond to unexpected texts about acting jobs or casting calls | Remember that legitimate talent agencies find jobs for you and pay you after the client pays them, rather than charging you upfront | Report unwanted texts to 7726 (SPAM) or use your phone's 'report junk' feature, then delete the message | Report the scam to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov | Independently verify any casting opportunity by contacting the studio or a known talent agency directly rather than using contact info from the text
Cited source: Military Consumer (FTC-affiliated), https://www.militaryconsumer.gov/blog/lights-camera-scam-spot-virtual-casting-call-scams
